layers.text: A kinsman-redeemer (go'el) was the near relative who bought back family land, and a related law had a man marry his dead brother's widow so that "his name will not be blotted out." Boaz does both at once, though exactly how these laws applied is debated.

The prophets use the same words for God. He is Israel's Redeemer (go'el), and in Ezekiel He says, "I spread My cloak over you," with the word kanaph, and "you became Mine." Ruth's request speaks the language of God's covenant love.

cites.at: Angie Velasquez Thornton, 3 Ways Ruth Foreshadows Christ, The Gospel Coalition Canada
John Currid, Ruth commentary, The Gospel Coalition

layers.text: Matthew names Boaz and Ruth in Jesus' family line. Many Christians see Boaz, the relative who willingly pays to redeem, as a picture of Christ, "born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law"; the New Testament does not draw the Boaz link itself.

passages.saying: The LORD will judge the ends of the earth and will give power to His king. He will exalt the horn of His anointed.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TBESH, the Septuagint, the NET Bible notes, the Talmud, OpenBible.info cross-references, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Hannah, childless and taunted by her rival, prays for a son and then gives him to the LORD's service. Her song of thanks praises a God who reverses fortunes: "He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap."

layers.evidence: Judges 21:25. TAHOT: mashiach occurs earlier only in Leviticus 4:3, 4:5, 4:16 and 6:22, of the priest. Ellicott and JFB on 1 Samuel 2:10 call this the first passage to speak of His Anointed, the Messiah. Septuagint: the horn of his christos
layers.text: Israel had no king yet, but Hannah ends with "His king" and "His anointed." Mashiach, the word behind Messiah, had so far been used only of "the anointed priest"; this is its first use for a king. The Greek Old Testament has christos.

layers.evidence: NET Bible note on 1 Samuel 1:20: a sound-play, not a strict etymology. TAHOT: sha'al (H7592) in 1:20, 1:28, 8:10 and 12:17. Keil and Delitzsch on 1:20 and 1:28; Gill on 1:20 and Fix and Vannoy (The Gospel Coalition) on the link with Saul

cites.at: S. A. Fix and J. Robert Vannoy, 1 Samuel commentary, The Gospel Coalition

layers.text: Hannah explains Samuel's name with a sound-play: "Because I have asked for him from the LORD" (sha'al, to ask). In 1:28 she calls him sha'ul, "asked" (BSB "dedicated"), spelled like the name Saul. Later Israel is "asking him for a king," and gets Saul.

layers.evidence: Ellicott, JFB, Benson and Poole on Luke 1:46; Gill and the Pulpit Commentary on 1 Samuel 2:1
layers.text: Mary's song in Luke 1 is modeled on Hannah's. Hannah: "My heart rejoices in the LORD"; Mary: "my spirit rejoices in God my Savior!" Hannah's God "humbles and He exalts"; Mary's "has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble."

layers.evidence: Fix and Vannoy (The Gospel Coalition) and the Reformation Study Bible note the frame. TAHOT: qeren, horn, in 1 Samuel 2:10 and 2 Samuel 22:3; mashiach in 2:10 and 22:51. Barnes and Gill on 1 Samuel 2:10 compare Luke 1:69

cites.at: S. A. Fix and J. Robert Vannoy, 1 Samuel commentary, The Gospel Coalition

layers.text: Hannah's song and David's song frame the books of Samuel. Both call God the Rock, sing of a "horn," and end with "His king" and "His anointed." Zechariah takes up the picture for Jesus: God "has raised up a horn of salvation for us" in David's house.

layers.evidence: Ellicott and Barnes on 1 Samuel 2:26 compare Luke 2:52
layers.text: Luke describes the boy Jesus in words close to those used of the boy Samuel. Samuel "continued to grow in stature and in favor with the LORD and with man"; Jesus "grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man."

layers.evidence: Talmud Megillah 14a, paraphrased. Keil and Delitzsch on 1 Samuel 2:10: David's line culminated in the Messiah; Pulpit: looking onwards to the Messiah, David's greater Son. TAHOT: qeren in 16:13 and 2:10; pakh, flask, in 10:1
layers.text: Hannah's son anointed Saul from "a flask of oil" but David with "the horn of oil," and Jewish tradition reads her "horn" as a prophecy of David's lasting line. Commentators see that line reaching forward to the Messiah.

passages.saying: The glory has departed from Israel
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: Israel took the ark of the covenant, the sacred chest that stood for God's presence, into battle to "save us from the hand of our enemies." They lost, the ark was captured and the priest Eli's sons died. Dying in childbirth, his daughter-in-law named her son.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: I-khavod (H0350) and kavod, glory (H3519), in 4:21; galah, go into exile (H1540), in 4:21 and 4:22. TBESH: no glory. The first part, i, can mean not or where?, so both senses are proposed.

cites.at: S. A. Fix and J. Robert Vannoy, 1 Samuel commentary, The Gospel Coalition

layers.text: Ichabod, i-khavod, means "no glory" or, as many read it, "where's the glory?" Her words explain it: "The glory has departed from Israel." Departed is galah, the verb for going into exile. The glory has been carried off like a captive.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: kaved, heavy (H3515), in 4:18; kavad, honor (H3513), in 2:29-30; kavod, glory (H3519), in 4:21-22. All share the root k-b-d, which has to do with weight. The warning in 2:27-30 comes through a man of God. Fix and Vannoy (The Gospel Coalition) trace this thread from 2:30 through chapters 4 to 6.

cites.at: S. A. Fix and J. Robert Vannoy, 1 Samuel commentary, The Gospel Coalition
S. A. Fix and J. Robert Vannoy, 1 Samuel commentary, The Gospel Coalition

layers.text: Glory, kavod, comes from a root meaning heavy. Eli died because he was "old and heavy" (kaved). Through a prophet God had warned him, "You have honored your sons more than Me," and "I will honor those who honor Me." Honor, too, comes from the "heavy" root.

layers.evidence: Psalm 78:60 names Shiloh, where the ark had stood (1 Samuel 4:3-4), and the next verse is widely read as the ark's capture: God's strength and splendor given into captivity.
layers.text: A psalm looks back on this day: God "abandoned the tabernacle of Shiloh" and "delivered His strength to captivity, and His splendor to the hand of the adversary." The same psalm ends with God choosing David to shepherd His people.

passages.saying: His name means Fool, and folly accompanies him.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: David's men had guarded the flocks of Nabal, a rich man "harsh and evil in his dealings." When David asked for food, Nabal insulted him, and David set out with 400 men to kill every male in Nabal's household. Nabal's wife Abigail rode out to stop him.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: Naval (H5037) and nevalah, folly (H5039), in 25:25; naval, fool (H5036), in Psalm 14:1. Benson: a fool not by nature but through pride and insolence; Keil and Delitzsch: folly goes with ungodliness. Ellicott takes the name as probably a nickname earned by his folly; Abigail hears only one sense.
layers.text: His own wife says it: Nabal means "fool," and folly, nevalah, goes with him. In Hebrew a nabal is not slow-witted but someone who lives as if God and others do not count: "The fool says in his heart, ‘There is no God.’"

layers.evidence: TAHOT: nivlei, skins of (H5035), in 25:18; betset hayyayin mi-Naval, when the wine had gone out from Nabal, in 25:37. Some commentators see a play between nevel and Naval; the text does not point it out.
layers.text: Some hear a second pun. Abigail packs "two skins of wine," and a skin or jar is nevel, close to Nabal. Where our English says "when Nabal was sober," the Hebrew says the wine had gone out of Nabal. On this reading the fool ends as an emptied wineskin.

passages.saying: He will build a house for My Name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT and TBESH, the Septuagint, the Dead Sea Scroll 4Q174 (Intertextual Bible), F. F. Bruce, OpenBible.info cross-references, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: King David, settled in a palace of cedar, wants to build a temple for the ark of God. Through the prophet Nathan, God turns the offer around: David's son will build the temple, and God will build David a dynasty and establish its throne forever.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: bayit (H1004) 15 times in 2 Samuel 7. TBESH: house, also household, family. The closing lesson is Keil and Delitzsch's on 7:11; Gill and Benson make the same turn
layers.text: The chapter turns on bayit, "house," used 15 times. David offers God a house, a temple; God answers, "He Himself will establish a house for you," a dynasty. One commentator draws the lesson: God must build a man's house before the man can build God's.

layers.evidence: Solomon adds: I have built the house for the Name of the LORD (1 Kings 8:20). Benson and Gill on 2 Samuel 7:14: the discipline clause fits Solomon, not Christ
layers.text: The first fulfillment is Solomon, who dedicated the temple saying, "Now the LORD has fulfilled the word that He spoke." The promise even allows for his failures: "When he does wrong, I will discipline him."

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch on 1 Chronicles 17:13: the omission comes from reading David's seed as the Messiah; Ellicott: probably not a mere abridgment; Barnes: the writer is not about to record Solomon's sins
layers.text: Chronicles retells the promise without "When he does wrong," and where Samuel has "Your house and kingdom," it reads "My house and My kingdom." Some commentators say Chronicles reads the son as the Messiah; others, that it simply passes over Solomon's sins.

layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary on Hebrews 1:5: a primary and partial fulfillment in Solomon; Gill and Bengel: spoken of Solomon, but belonging to Christ. Barnes on 2 Samuel 7:14: Hebrews 1:5 applies it to Christ
layers.text: Hebrews quotes "I will be His Father, and He will be My Son" of Christ, and the angel tells Mary her son will have "the throne of His father David" and "His kingdom will never end!" Commentators see in Solomon only a first, partial fulfillment.

layers.evidence: 4Q174 (4QFlorilegium) on 2 Samuel 7:11-14, read with Amos 9:11 through the shared verb qum (TAHOT; BSB restore), in the Intertextual Bible translation with a note by Reed Carlson. F. F. Bruce (Encyclopaedia Judaica) on the same text
layers.text: The Dead Sea Scrolls show Jews reading this as a promise of a coming king. One scroll applies it to the Branch of David and links "I will raise up" to Amos's "I will restore the fallen tent of David," the same verb in Hebrew. Acts 15:16 quotes Amos.

layers.evidence: Numbers 12:7. Mary Rose D'Angelo argues that Hebrews 3 draws on 1 Chronicles 17:14; Erich Grässer disputes it. Septuagint: pistoso auton en oiko mou; pistoo there means establish (Abbott-Smith; Brenton). Ellicott on Hebrews 3:6: Moses faithful as a servant in God's house, Christ as a son over it
layers.text: Hebrews sets Moses, faithful "in all My house," beside the Son: "Christ is faithful as the Son over God’s house." Some scholars also hear 1 Chronicles 17:14, where in Greek God establishes David's son in His house with a verb from the root for "faithful."

passages.saying: Then Elijah took the child, brought him down from the upper room into the house, and gave him to his mother.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT and TBESH, the Septuagint, OpenBible.info cross-references, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Gill on 1 Kings 17:22: the first instance of anyone raised from the dead
layers.text: During a famine Elijah stays with a widow in Zarephath. When her son dies, Elijah stretches himself over the boy and prays, and the LORD restores his life: the first raising of the dead in the Bible. His mother says, "Now I know that you are a man of God."

layers.evidence: Both read kai edoken auton te metri autou: the Septuagint of 1 Kings 17:23 and Luke 7:15 in every edition TAGNT records. Ellicott and JFB on Luke 7:16 recall Elijah
layers.text: Luke tells how Jesus raised a widow's only son at Nain in the words of Elijah's story. Both stories meet a widow at the town gate, and Luke's Greek for "Jesus gave him back to his mother" matches the Greek Old Testament of this verse word for word.

layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary on Luke 7:14: unlike Elijah and Elisha, who mourned and agonized in prayer, the Lord raised the dead with one word. Edersheim contrasts Christ's calm with the intense agitation of an Elijah or an Elisha

cites.at: Alfred Edersheim, The Life and Times of Jesus the Messiah, Book III, chapter 20

layers.text: The differences matter too. Elijah "stretched himself out over the child three times" and pleaded with the LORD; Jesus only touches the coffin and speaks: "Young man," He said, "I tell you, get up!" The crowd cries, "A great prophet has appeared among us!"

layers.evidence: Ellicott, JFB and Barnes on Luke 4:26: a Gentile, Phoenician town between Tyre and Sidon; Ellicott sees in it the future calling of the Gentiles
layers.text: Jesus Himself pointed to this widow at Nazareth: "Elijah was not sent to any of them, but to the widow of Zarephath in Sidon," a Gentile town. He named Naaman the Syrian too, and the synagogue crowd was so enraged that it tried to throw Him off a cliff.

layers.evidence: Edersheim on Nain: southwards lies Shunem. JFB on Luke 7:16: more than bringing back the days of Elijah and Elisha. Barnes, JFB, Gill and the Pulpit Commentary on Hebrews 11:35 name the widow of Zarephath and the Shunammite

cites.at: Alfred Edersheim, The Life and Times of Jesus the Messiah, Book III, chapter 20

layers.text: Elisha later raised a mother's son at Shunem, near Nain, so Luke's story recalls both prophets. Most commentators read Hebrews' "Women received back their dead, raised to life again" as the widow of Zarephath and the woman of Shunem.

layers.evidence: TBESH: Elijah, my God is Jehovah, or Yah is God. Barnes on 1 Kings 17:1: the name expresses the truth his whole life preached. Pulpit on 1 Kings 18:39: the people turned the prophet's name into a war cry
layers.text: Elijah's name, Eli-yahu, means that the LORD is my God. At Carmel the people's verdict puts his name into words: "The LORD, He is God! The LORD, He is God!" The name sums up the truth his whole life preached.

passages.saying: But I know that my Redeemer lives, and in the end He will stand upon the earth.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT and TBESH, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, the Septuagint, 1 Clement, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Job 19:25: Job knows he will be vindicated, and though he will die, his vindicator lives; the picture is of God rising up to do justice.
layers.text: Job has lost his children, wealth and health, and his friends insist the innocent never perish. Wishing his words were "chiseled in stone forever," he declares that his Redeemer lives and will rise up for him in the end, even if Job himself dies.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Job 1:9 and 2:3: chinnam means gratis, from the verb chanan (to be gracious) or the noun chen (grace). TBESH H2600: freely, for nothing, without cause.
layers.text: The accuser asks, "Does Job fear God for nothing?" Later God says, "you incited Me against him to ruin him without cause." Both are one Hebrew word, chinnam, related to the word for grace. Will Job fear God for nothing while he suffers for nothing?

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Job 1:6: with the article, the word's meaning gets prominence. TBESH H7854: adversary, one who withstands. Barnes and the Pulpit Commentary on Job 1:6 set it beside Revelation 12:10; Ellicott notes the article occurs only here and in Zechariah.
layers.text: Here Satan is ha-satan, "the adversary," the "the" stressing what the word means. He questions Job's motives before God. Revelation celebrates the end of that role: "the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down," a scene set beside Job 1 and Zechariah 3.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Job 16:19: the witness in heaven must be God. Matthew Henry, Gill and JFB on Job 9:33 read it of Christ. Barnes: Job did not desire a mediator in the sense in which we understand that word.
layers.text: Job's hope grows: "Nor is there a mediator between us," then "my witness is in heaven, and my advocate is on high." Christians hear the answer in "one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." Others think Job asks only for an umpire to hear his case.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Job 19:25: go'el, from ga'al (to redeem, protect, vindicate); here Job thinks of God as his vindicator. NET on Proverbs 23:11: the LORD is probably the protector there. Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary: Job here names God his Goel. TBESH H1350.
layers.text: "Redeemer" is go'el, the next of kin who could "redeem what his brother has sold" and was "the avenger of blood." Proverbs probably gives the title to God as defender of orphans: "their Redeemer is strong." Job, too, surely means God Himself.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Job 19:25: an adjective here, an epithet of the vindicator. TBESH H0314: later, latter, last. Keil and Delitzsch render it as the last One; JFB and Poole link it with the First and the Last; the Pulpit Commentary allows at the last.
layers.text: "In the end" is acharon, "last," perhaps a title: the Redeemer is the Last. Isaiah pairs the same two words for God, "Redeemer" and "I am the last," and the risen Jesus says, "I am the First and the Last." Others read it simply as "at the last."

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Job 19:26: the phrase can mean without my flesh or in my flesh. Septuagint (Rahlfs) of 19:26: anastēsai, raise up my skin. 1 Clement 24 and 26: Christ the firstfruits, and Job cited for the raising of this flesh. Barnes sees no necessary reference to resurrection.

cites.at: Clement of Rome, First Epistle to the Corinthians 26

layers.text: Verse 26 is hard: the Hebrew "from my flesh" can mean with it or without it. The Greek Old Testament has God raise up Job's skin, and an early Christian writer who calls the risen Jesus the firstfruits cites Job for the raising of our flesh.

passages.saying: You are My Son; today I have become Your Father.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, the Septuagint, Jerome, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Psalm 2:7: ancient Near Eastern adoption language from covenants of grant, in which a lord rewarded a faithful subject with the status of son and an inheritance.
layers.text: Kings plot "against the LORD and against His Anointed One," but God has installed His King on Zion, calls him Son and promises him the nations. This is royal adoption language, used of David's line: a faithful subject made a son, with an inheritance.

layers.evidence: Bengel on Acts 4:27: Herod answers to the psalm's kings and Pilate to its rulers; Gill and JFB apply the psalm to Jesus. TAHOT and TAGNT: mashiach (H4899), christos (G5547), chriō (G5548).
layers.text: When the apostles are threatened, the church prays this psalm as current events: Herod and Pilate conspired "against Your holy servant Jesus, whom You anointed." The psalm's "Anointed One" is mashiach (Messiah), in Greek christos (Christ).

layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary on Acts 13:33: this use of the psalm is best explained by Romans 1:4. Poole: Christ did not begin to be Son at the resurrection but was then shown to be.
layers.text: Paul hears the king's "today" as resurrection day: God kept His promise "by raising up Jesus." In Romans, Jesus is "declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection," shown to be Son then, not made Son. Hebrews quotes it too.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Luke 3:22: the words recall Psalm 2:7 and Isaiah 42:1; one Greek manuscript (D), several Latin ones and some church fathers quote Psalm 2:7 in full, against the weight of the manuscripts. Ellicott and Pulpit on Matthew 3:17.
layers.text: At Jesus' baptism the voice from heaven says, "You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased," recalling this psalm and Isaiah's Servant, "in whom My soul delights." In Luke, a few old copies read the psalm's "today I have become Your Father" instead.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Psalm 2:9: the Septuagint reads the consonants as ra'ah (shepherd) rather than ra'a' (break); nafats (smash) in the next line favors break. TAGNT: poimainō in Revelation 2:27, 12:5, 19:15 and 7:17.
layers.text: The Hebrew letters of "You will break them with an iron scepter" can also read "you will shepherd," as the Greek Old Testament took it. Revelation quotes it so (BSB "rule"), and the Lamb "will be their shepherd." But "shatter them like pottery" favors "break."

layers.evidence: Ellicott on Psalm 2:12: bar for son occurs in Hebrew only in Proverbs 31:2; the Septuagint, followed by the Vulgate, has lay hold of discipline. Keil and Delitzsch and the NET Bible notes give bar as pure. Jerome, Apology against Rufinus 1.19: Adore the Son in his commentary, Worship purely in his Psalter.

cites.at: Jerome, Apology against Rufinus 1.19

layers.text: "Kiss the Son" uses bar, Aramaic for son, where verse 7 has the Hebrew ben; elsewhere Hebrew has bar only in Proverbs 31:2. Some read "pure"; the Greek urges taking hold of instruction. Jerome rendered it both ways, as adoring the Son and as worshiping purely.

passages.saying: what is man that You are mindful of him, or the son of man that You care for him?
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB and its footnotes, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Psalm 8:5: these terms allude to mankind's royal status as God's vice-regents.
layers.text: Looking at "the moon and the stars," David marvels that God cares for frail humans at all, yet has crowned them "with glory and honor" and made them rulers over the animals, as in Genesis 1. These are royal words: humans rule on God's behalf.

layers.evidence: TBESH: enosh, man, mortal man; adam, man, human being. Barnes on Hebrews 2:9: we do not see mankind with the dominion the psalm describes.
layers.text: Hebrews quotes this and admits the gap: "Yet at present we do not see everything subject to him. But we see Jesus." In the psalm "son of man" (ben adam) means a human being, like enosh, "mortal man." What God promised humanity is already true of one man.

layers.evidence: BSB footnote on Psalm 8:5: or than God, or than the heavenly beings; see also the Septuagint. NET Bible notes: Hebrews 2:7 follows the Septuagint. TBESG (Abbott-Smith) on brachy ti cites Hebrews 2:7, 9 for both senses. Bengel and Gill on Hebrews 2:7 read time; Barnes, JFB and Ellicott, rank.
layers.text: In "a little lower than the angels" the Hebrew has elohim, "God" or "the heavenly beings"; Hebrews follows the Greek "angels." Its Greek for "a little" can mean slightly or for a short time, so some read Jesus' lowering as brief, others as a matter of rank.

layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary on 1 Corinthians 15:27: words spoken of man in general are transferred to the federal Head of humanity. Ellicott: all things are put under man, and in a higher sense under the Son of Man.
layers.text: Paul joins "You have placed everything under his feet" to Christ's reign: "He must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death." The rule given to humanity belongs, in a higher sense, to Christ, the new Adam.

layers.evidence: BSB footnote on Psalm 8:2: literally strength; the Septuagint has praise, cited in Matthew 21:16. Abbott-Smith (TBESG) marks Matthew 21:16 as the Septuagint's wording. Pulpit Commentary on Matthew 21:16: words first applied to Jehovah, which Jesus claims as addressed to Himself.
layers.text: Children shout "Hosanna to the Son of David!" and leaders object. Matthew gives Jesus' answer in the Greek Old Testament's words: "From the mouths of children and infants You have ordained praise." The Hebrew has "strength." Jesus accepts praise meant for God.

passages.saying: For You will not abandon my soul to Sheol, nor will You let Your Holy One see decay.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, Josephus, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Psalm 16:10: the psalmist speaks of himself, confident that God will prevent him from dying.
layers.text: David trusts the LORD as his "chosen portion," so he is sure God will not hand him over to the grave but show him "the path of life," with "eternal pleasures at Your right hand." He is confident God will keep him from death.

At Pentecost Peter quotes the psalm and argues it cannot mean David: "David died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day." As a prophet, David foresaw "the resurrection of the Christ, that He was not abandoned to Hades, nor did His body see decay."

layers.evidence: Josephus, Antiquities 7.15.3 (Whiston): Hyrcanus the high priest opened one room of David's tomb and took out three thousand talents; many years later King Herod opened another.
layers.text: David's tomb was a landmark. Nehemiah marks repairs "opposite the tombs of David," and an ancient historian says a high priest and later King Herod each took treasure from a room of it. Everyone knew where David lay. But "God has raised this Jesus to life."

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Psalm 16:10: shachat, pit, often a title for Sheol. TBESH H7845: Pit, another name of Sheol. TBESG (Abbott-Smith) G1312: corruption of the grave; in the Septuagint chiefly for shachat.
layers.text: "Decay" is the Hebrew shachat, "pit," a name for the grave; the Greek Old Testament has diaphthora, "corruption." Both promise rescue from death. Paul draws the contrast: David "saw decay. But the One whom God raised from the dead did not see decay."

layers.evidence: Ellicott and JFB on Psalm 16:10: chasid is one who receives God's grace and shows it. Ellicott on Acts 13:34: the Greek for mercies is the adjective translated holy in the next verse; Pulpit: hosia stands for the Hebrew chasadim. Gill: the blessings are made sure only by His resurrection.
layers.text: Paul links two verses by one Greek word. Isaiah's "loving devotion promised to David" (chesed) is in Greek the "holy" (hosia) blessings; the psalm's "Holy One" is chasid, one who shows chesed, in Greek hosios. The promises are sure in God's risen Holy One.

passages.saying: My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: David cries out to a God who seems silent while enemies surround him, then turns to praise: God has listened, and the nations will worship.
On the cross Jesus cries the psalm's first line in Aramaic: "Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?"

layers.evidence: On Matthew 27:47, Ellicott and Benson lean to a mishearing; Barnes, Gill and Matthew Henry to mockery; the Pulpit Commentary calls it an undecided question.
layers.text: Some bystanders say He is calling Elijah. Commentators differ on whether they misheard "Eloi" (my God) or mocked Him. Either way, the cry was the opening line of a psalm.
The psalm's details return at the cross: mockers shake their heads and say God should deliver Him, and soldiers divide His garments and cast lots, which John says fulfilled Scripture.

The psalm does not end in despair. Its second half praises God among "my brothers," words Hebrews puts in Jesus' mouth, and it ends with all nations turning to the LORD. Many readers think quoting the first line called the whole psalm to mind.

layers.evidence: STEPBible's TAHOT gives the Leningrad Codex reading ka'ari and notes the Judean Desert reading ka'aru
layers.text: The BSB reads "they have pierced my hands and feet." The traditional Hebrew text has ka'ari, "like a lion," while a manuscript found in the Judean Desert reads ka'aru, "they dug." Christians link the verse to the nail wounds, but the wording is a real textual question.

passages.saying: Even my close friend whom I trusted, the one who shared my bread, has lifted up his heel against me.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the Septuagint, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes on Psalm 41:9: the figure is a horse that turns and kicks the one who fed it; the Pulpit Commentary reads it the same way.
layers.text: Sick in bed, David hears his enemies ask, "When will he die and be forgotten?" Worse, a trusted friend who ate at his table has turned against him, like a horse kicking the one who fed it. David asks God to "raise me up."

At the Last Supper Jesus applies the verse to Judas: "The one who shares My bread has lifted up his heel against Me." Soon after, "He dipped the morsel and gave it to Judas." The friend who shared the psalmist's bread now sits at Jesus' own table.

layers.evidence: The Septuagint of Psalm 41:9 has esthiō; John 13:18 has trōgō (TAGNT), used of eating Christ's flesh in John 6 and elsewhere in the New Testament only in Matthew 24:38. TBESG (Abbott-Smith) G5176: in late everyday Greek, simply to eat. The psalm's Hebrew has the ordinary akal, to eat (TAHOT), so the link to John 6 is in John's Greek.
layers.text: In John's Greek the word for "shares" (eats) is trōgō, not the Greek psalm's verb. John also uses it in "Whoever eats My flesh and drinks My blood has eternal life," though it was an everyday word. The betrayer ate with "the bread that came down from heaven."

layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary on Psalm 41:9: Ahithophel almost certainly intended; Poole and Barnes agree. Ellicott on Matthew 27:5: apanchō is the Septuagint's word in 2 Samuel 17:23. TAGNT: G0519 occurs only in Matthew 27:5.
layers.text: Many take David's false friend to be Ahithophel, who sided with Absalom and later "hanged himself." Matthew says Judas "went away and hanged himself," with a verb used nowhere else in the New Testament: the Greek Old Testament's word for Ahithophel.

layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary, Barnes, Gill and Benson on John 18:1 recall David's flight from Absalom; Benson calls David here a type of Christ.
layers.text: Betrayed by Ahithophel, David "crossed the Kidron Valley" and climbed the Mount of Olives weeping. Betrayed by Judas, Jesus "went out with His disciples across the Kidron Valley" to the same hill. Some recall David's flight here, though John himself does not point it out.

layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary on John 13:19: instead of shaking their faith, it will prove He was taken by no surprise. Ellicott: they will find in it confirmation of their faith in Him as the Messiah.
layers.text: Jesus names the betrayal in advance on purpose: "I am telling you now before it happens, so that when it comes to pass, you will believe that I am He." What could have shaken their faith becomes a reason for it.

layers.evidence: Bengel on John 13:18 compares aqev in Genesis 3:15. TAHOT tags both words H6119.
layers.text: "Heel" is aqev, the word of the first promise, where the serpent "will strike his heel" but the woman's seed "will crush your head." Some set the two verses side by side, and John notes that when Judas took the morsel, "Satan entered into him."

passages.saying: zeal for Your house has consumed me, and the insults of those who insult You have fallen on me.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, the Septuagint, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: JFB, introduction to Psalm 69: referred to seven times in the New Testament as prophetical of Christ and the gospel times.
layers.text: David, sinking into "deep waters," cries to God. He suffers "for Your sake": his devotion to God's house has made him "a stranger to my brothers." Yet the psalm ends in praise. The New Testament quotes it again and again of Christ.

layers.evidence: Ellicott on John 2:17: the change from past to future is itself significant. Bengel and Gill: His zeal at last cost Him His life. TAGNT: the future kataphagetai is in all major Greek texts; the Textus Receptus has the past.
layers.text: When Jesus clears the temple, His disciples remember the line "Zeal for Your house will consume Me." The psalm says "has consumed"; John has the future, "will consume." Some hear His death in that change: His zeal would cost Him His life.

Paul quotes the second half to teach patience with weaker believers: "even Christ did not please Himself." The insults aimed at God fell on Christ, so the strong can "bear with the shortcomings of the weak."

layers.evidence: Septuagint (Rahlfs) of Psalm 69:21: cholē and oxos. Benson, Gill and the Pulpit Commentary on Psalm 69:21 see it fulfilled at the cross; Gill links Matthew 27:34 and John 19:28. Benson and Gill also cite Psalm 22:15.
layers.text: David's enemies "poisoned my food with gall and gave me vinegar to quench my thirst," in Greek cholē and oxos. On the cross Jesus said "I am thirsty" to fulfill Scripture and was given oxos, sour wine; Matthew says He was first offered wine "mixed with gall."

layers.evidence: TAHOT: chinnam (H2600) in Psalm 69:4, Psalm 35:19 and Job 2:3; John 15:25 has dōrean (G1432). NET Bible notes on Job 2:3: chinnam means gratis, without cause.
layers.text: Jesus applies the psalm's "Those who hate me without cause" to His own enemies: "They hated Me without reason." Psalm 35:19 has the same Hebrew. The key word is chinnam, "for nothing," the word God uses of Job's undeserved suffering.

layers.evidence: Gill and Barnes on Psalm 69:25 note that Acts 1:20 applies it to Judas. JFB and Poole on Psalm 69 read David, suffering in God's cause, as a type of Christ; Matthew Henry reads its curses as prophecies of the destruction of Christ's persecutors.
layers.text: Peter applies verse 25 to Judas, turning "their place" into "his place." Older commentators read David, who suffered for God's sake, as a type of Christ, and the psalm's curses as falling on those who rejected Him.

passages.saying: Then I was a skilled craftsman at His side, and His delight day by day, rejoicing always in His presence.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB and its footnotes, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, the Septuagint, the Wisdom of Solomon, Athanasius, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Wisdom is pictured as a woman calling out "beside the gates to the city." She says she was with God before creation, "I was there when He established the heavens," and promises, "whoever finds me finds life."

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Proverbs 8:22: two Hebrew roots qanah, to possess and to create (Genesis 14:19; Deuteronomy 32:6). BSB footnote: or possessed. Athanasius, Discourse II Against the Arians 1 and 11.

cites.at: Athanasius, Discourse II Against the Arians 1

layers.text: "The LORD created me" uses qanah, which can mean "to possess" or "to create," as when God is "Creator of heaven and earth." Arius read "created" to make the Son a creature; Athanasius said it speaks of the Word becoming man. Both read Wisdom as the Son.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Proverbs 8:30: master craftsman or nursing child; craftsman has the most support (Septuagint, Vulgate, Syriac). TBESH: amon, skilled workman; sachaq, to laugh, play.
layers.text: "Skilled craftsman" is amon, a rare word: "master craftsman" or "nursing child." A child fits Wisdom being "brought forth," but craftsman has more support. "Rejoicing" is sachaq, "to laugh, play": Wisdom delights before God and "in the sons of men."

layers.evidence: Septuagint (Rahlfs) of Proverbs 8:23: en archē. Benson, Gill and Poole on John 1:1 point to Proverbs 8.
layers.text: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God" recalls Genesis 1 and also Wisdom, at God's side "from the beginning, before the earth began." The Greek of 8:23 even has John's opening words, en archē. But John goes further: "the Word was God."

layers.evidence: TAGNT: apaugasma occurs in the New Testament only at Hebrews 1:3. TBESG (Abbott-Smith) G0541: in the Septuagint only at Wisdom of Solomon 7:26, a book not in the Hebrew Bible, where Wisdom is the apaugasma of eternal light and the eikōn of God's goodness. Ellicott, Gill and JFB on Hebrews 1:3 compare it; JFB and Gill also point to Colossians 1:15.
layers.text: Hebrews calls the Son "the radiance of God’s glory." The Greek Old Testament has that word only in the Wisdom of Solomon, a book outside the Hebrew Bible: Wisdom is the radiance of eternal light and image of God's goodness. Paul calls the Son God's "image."

layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary on Luke 11:49: He identifies Himself with the Wisdom of God; Barnes and Gill agree. Gill notes some have thought a lost book of that name is cited; Ellicott finds no trace of one.
layers.text: Paul calls Christ "the power of God and the wisdom of God." In Luke, Jesus quotes "the wisdom of God": "I will send them prophets and apostles." In Matthew He says it in His own voice: "I am sending you prophets." Many hear Him speaking as God's Wisdom.

passages.saying: A good name is better than fine perfume
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.evidence: Readers take the startling line in more than one way. Jamieson, Fausset and Brown and the Pulpit Commentary tie it to the first half: death is better for one who has a good name. Keil and Delitzsch hear the same lament as Ecclesiastes 4:2. The verse does not explain itself.
layers.text: The Teacher sets a good name above costly perfume, then says something startling: "one’s day of death is better than his day of birth." He explains that "death is the end of every man," and the living should take it to heart.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: shem, name (H8034), and shemen, oil (H8081), side by side, each with tov, good. The BSB renders shemen here as perfume. Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, Keil and Delitzsch, Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary all note the sound-play; Gill adds that a good name is more lasting.
layers.text: The proverb is a sound-play: tov shem mishshemen tov, a good name (shem) is better than good oil (shemen). Perfume was scented oil and costly, yet a good name is worth more. Many add that a name lasts when the scent is gone.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: shemen (H8081) and shemekha, your name (H8034), two words apart in Song of Solomon 1:3: shemen turaq shemekha, oil poured out is your name. The verse begins lereach shemanekha tovim, the fragrance of your oils is good, so tov, shemen and shem all meet here, as in Ecclesiastes 7:1.
layers.text: The Song of Solomon makes the same pun as praise: "your name is like perfume poured out." In Hebrew it is shemen, then shemekha, "your name." The two words sound so alike that Scripture pairs them twice, here and in Ecclesiastes 7:1.

passages.saying: Set me as a seal over your heart, as a seal upon your arm. For love is as strong as death
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TBESH, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, the Mishnah (Joshua Kulp's translation), and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Ellicott on Song 8:6: the seal is a symbol of something especially dear and precious. The Pulpit Commentary: the signet ring was sometimes carried by a string on the breast, near the heart.
layers.text: The bride asks to be worn as a seal on her beloved's heart and arm, kept close as something precious. Love like this cannot be put out or bought: "Mighty waters cannot quench love; rivers cannot sweep it away." Earlier she sang, "My beloved is mine and I am his."

layers.evidence: TBESH: shalhevet, flame; Yah, a shortened form of the LORD's name. TAHOT glosses it a flame of the Lord. NET Bible notes: the Masoretes did not point it as the divine name; most likely an intensive. Ellicott: the only sacred name in the book, used as a superlative. Gill: a superlative, or a flame kindled by the Lord himself.
layers.text: "The fiercest blaze of all" is one Hebrew word, shalhevetyah: "flame" plus -yah, which may be Yah, short for God's name, its only trace in the Song. Many read it as a way of saying mightiest, as the BSB does; others hear a flame kindled by God.

layers.evidence: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown: the Jews explain the Song of the union of Jehovah and ancient Israel; the Targum on the Song reads it that way. Gill: the ancient Jews called it the Holy of Holies, citing Mishnah Yadayim 3:5, Rabbi Akiva (trans. Joshua Kulp, CC BY).
layers.text: Jewish readers long heard more than a love poem: the oldest readings take it as a picture of God and Israel. When rabbis debated which books were holy, Rabbi Akiva answered that all the writings are holy, but the Song of Songs is the holy of holies.

The prophets already picture God as Israel's husband: "I will betroth you to Me forever," in "loving devotion"; "as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you"; "I remember the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride."

layers.evidence: Benson and Gill read the Song as Christ's marriage with the church, and Jamieson, Fausset and Brown note that Christians explain it of Christ and the Church.
layers.text: John the Baptist says, "The bride belongs to the bridegroom"; Jesus calls Himself the bridegroom; Paul applies marriage to "Christ and the church"; Revelation has "the marriage of the Lamb." Christians came to read the Song in this light.

layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary on Song 8:6 recalls Paul in Romans 8. Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary: no waters can quench Christ's love to us.
layers.text: Christians hear in love "as strong as death" a love stronger still. Some recall Paul here: neither death nor life "will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord." Others add that no waters can quench Christ's love.

passages.saying: He looked for justice, but saw bloodshed; for righteousness, but heard a cry of distress.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: Isaiah sings about a vineyard its owner tended with every care, which still grew only sour grapes. Then he names it: the vineyard is Israel, and the fruit God wanted was justice.

The punchline is two pairs of sound-alike words: God looked for mishpat (justice) and found mispach (bloodshed), for tsedaqah (righteousness) and heard tse'aqah (a cry). Mispach occurs nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible, so its exact sense is not certain.

Tse'aqah is the cry God heard from the slaves in Egypt and the outcry against Sodom, and Isaiah has already called Jerusalem's rulers "rulers of Sodom." God's own people now cause the cry He once rescued them from.
Israel as God's vine is a running picture: "You uprooted a vine from Egypt; You drove out the nations and transplanted it."

Jesus retells this song as the parable of the tenants, with Isaiah's details: a planted vineyard, a wall, a wine vat, a watchtower. This time the owner sends his beloved son, and the leaders know the story is about them.
Jesus says, "I am the true vine." Where the vineyard of Isaiah 5 gave sour fruit, the true vine bears fruit, and those who remain in Him "bear much fruit."

passages.saying: If you do not stand firm in your faith, then you will not stand at all.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, the Septuagint, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Two kings march on Jerusalem, and King Ahaz and his people tremble "like trees in the forest shaken by the wind." God sends Isaiah to say the invasion "will not happen." All turns on whether Ahaz will trust God, and he refuses even the sign God offers.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Isaiah 7:9: a wordplay designed to draw attention to the alternatives set before the king; ta'aminu is the Hiphil and te'amenu the Niphal of aman. TBESH H0539: Niphal made firm, sure; Hiphil to trust, believe.
layers.text: The warning uses one Hebrew verb twice: im lo ta'aminu ki lo te'amenu. Ta'aminu, "believe," and te'amenu, "be made firm," are two forms of aman. The pun sets the king's two choices side by side, and the BSB keeps the echo: "stand firm" and "stand at all."

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch on Isaiah 7:9: the same play upon words is in 2 Chronicles 20:20. Ellicott: an affirmative way of putting Isaiah's words to Ahaz. Maclaren: believing and being established are two forms of the same root-word.
layers.text: Earlier, King Jehoshaphat faced an invasion with the same pair: "Believe in the LORD your God, and you will be upheld" (ha'aminu, te'amenu), Isaiah's warning put positively. His people sang, and "the LORD set ambushes" against the invaders.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: the first occurrence of H0539 is Genesis 15:6 (vehe'emin). Keil and Delitzsch: aman is to be firm and to confirm, in Hiphil to trust, believe. Gill: this is the first time we read of believing.
layers.text: Aman first appears in the Bible when "Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness," the verse Paul quotes in Romans and Galatians. Isaiah's pun shows what the word holds: in Hebrew, believing God and being made firm share one root.

layers.evidence: Septuagint of Isaiah 28:16: ho pisteuōn ep' autō ou mē kataischynthē. TAHOT: ha-ma'amin is H0539.
layers.text: Isaiah's stone in Zion uses the word again: ha-ma'amin, "the one who believes will never be shaken." The Greek Old Testament reads "put to shame," and Paul and Peter quote it of Christ: "the one who believes in Him will never be put to shame."

layers.evidence: TBESG G0281: amen, from aman, be firm. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch: Isaiah 65:16 is literally the God of Amen, and Ellicott hears an echo of it in Revelation 3:14. Keil and Delitzsch link it to 2 Corinthians 1:20. Barnes: Amen means true, certain, faithful.
layers.text: Amen comes from the same root, "be firm." Isaiah's "God of truth" is literally the God of Amen, and Jesus takes Amen as His title: "the Amen, the faithful and true Witness." So, Paul says, all God's promises are "Yes" in Christ.

passages.saying: Behold, the virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son, and will call Him Immanuel.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, Ligonier articles, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Two kings march on Jerusalem, and King Ahaz and his people tremble "like trees in the forest shaken by the wind." Isaiah offers him any sign he wants; Ahaz refuses to ask, so the Lord gives a sign anyway: a son to be called Immanuel.

layers.evidence: TBESH H6005: Immanuel, God with us. TAHOT writes the name as two words in 7:14 and 8:8, the same two words (H5973, H0410) that end 8:10.
layers.text: Immanuel is Hebrew for "God with us," as Matthew translates. Isaiah keeps sounding the name: the Assyrian flood will cover "your entire land, O Immanuel!" and the next oracle ends, "For God is with us," in Hebrew the same two words, immanu el.

layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary, giving Bishop Lowth's view: a double bearing and a double fulfillment. JFB: partly the immediate event, fully the Messiah. Gill: a sign of present deliverance. NET Bible notes on Isaiah 7:14 and 7:16.
layers.text: The sign had a near horizon. Before the boy could "reject evil and choose good," the two kings' lands would be laid waste, and soon Assyria took Damascus. Isaiah's next son gets a similar timetable (8:4). So many readers see a double fulfillment, near and far.

layers.evidence: Ellicott: almah strictly denotes one of marriageable age. Barnes: the word is used of Rebekah, and the Septuagint has parthenos. Gill: the Jewish translators of the Septuagint so rendered it long before Matthew. Jamieson, Fausset and Brown: from a root to lie hid. TBESG (Abbott-Smith) G3933: parthenos renders almah at Genesis 24:43 and Isaiah 7:14.
layers.text: Matthew quotes this verse of Jesus' birth. Isaiah's word almah means a young woman of marriageable age, and the Greek Old Testament had already rendered it parthenos, "virgin," here and for Rebekah in Genesis 24:43. Its root means hidden, of a maiden kept from men's gaze.

layers.evidence: Barnes and Ellicott on Isaiah 9:6: the name is applied to the LORD Himself in 10:21. Keil and Delitzsch: the same person as the son of the virgin in chapter 7. TAHOT: El Gibbor is H0410 and H1368 in both verses.
layers.text: Two chapters on, the child returns: "unto us a son is given," named "Mighty God," El Gibbor, who will "reign on the throne of David." A chapter later Isaiah uses El Gibbor of the LORD Himself: a remnant will return "to the Mighty God."

layers.evidence: Gerald Bilkes and Gerrit Scott Dawson (Ligonier) tie Jesus' closing promise in Matthew 28:20, "I am with you always," to His name Immanuel, God with us (Matthew 1:23).

cites.at: Gerald Bilkes, Immanuel (Ligonier)
Gerrit Scott Dawson, I Am with You Always (Ligonier)

layers.text: Matthew gives the name near his start, "God with us," and Jesus' last words echo it: "surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age." In between He promises, "where two or three gather together in My name, there am I with them."

layers.evidence: Ellicott on Hebrews 2:13: the words are from Isaiah 8:18, with Isaiah representing Christ. The Pulpit Commentary: Isaiah is himself a sign, a type of the Immanuel to come. Gill and Jamieson, Fausset and Brown also trace the words to Isaiah 8:18.
layers.text: Isaiah says he and his children are "signs and symbols in Israel," and Hebrews puts his words in Christ's mouth: "Here am I, and the children God has given Me." The prophet's sign-children become a picture of Christ and the family He brings to God.

passages.saying: He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him, and by His stripes we are healed.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the Targum of Isaiah, and commentaries on Bible Hub.

layers.text: Isaiah describes the LORD's servant suffering for wrongs that are not His own. Watch the pronouns: the wounds are His, the transgressions are ours, and the peace and the healing come to us.

layers.evidence: Peter's word is molops, a bruise or wound left by a blow (TBESG, from Abbott-Smith). It is the word the Greek Old Testament uses here, and it appears nowhere else in the New Testament. Isaiah's chabburah is a bruise or welt (TBESH). Ellicott on Isaiah 53:5 links Peter's use to the slaves he addressed, who were scourged.
layers.text: Peter quotes this line to household servants who could be beaten even for doing good: "By His stripes you are healed." Isaiah's "we" becomes "you," and Peter's word for stripes means a welt, a mark many of his readers knew on their own backs.

layers.evidence: Isaiah 53:4 has choli, sickness, and makob, pain (TBESH); the Greek Old Testament renders the first as sins. Barnes and the Pulpit Commentary on Matthew 8:17: Matthew follows the Hebrew; Barnes: the word for griefs properly means diseases of the body.
layers.text: The New Testament reads this song two ways at once. Matthew quotes 53:4 of Jesus' healings, where the Hebrew speaks of sickness. The Greek Old Testament made it sins, and Peter writes, "He Himself bore our sins." The Servant carries both.

"Crushed" is the Hebrew daka, and it returns five verses later: "it was the LORD’s will to crush Him." Onlookers thought God was striking Him (53:4). The chapter answers that He was crushed for our iniquities, and that even this served God's purpose.

layers.evidence: Gill, the Pulpit Commentary and Ellicott on Luke 22:37.
layers.text: On His last night Jesus applies the chapter to Himself: "this Scripture must be fulfilled in Me," He says, and quotes 53:12, "He was numbered with the transgressors." The next day He was crucified between two criminals.

layers.evidence: Gill on Acts 8:34 reports Jews who apply the passage to the people of Israel in general. See also Barnes and the Pulpit Commentary on Acts 8:34.
layers.text: An Ethiopian official asked, "who is the prophet talking about, himself or someone else?" Isaiah calls Israel God's servant (49:3), and medieval Jewish commentators read the song that way. Yet this Servant is "stricken for the transgression of My people." Philip answered with Jesus.

layers.evidence: Targum Jonathan on Isaiah 52:13 and 53:5 (English translation of 1871, on Sefaria). TBESH lists both senses of chalal, to pierce and to profane
layers.text: An early Jewish paraphrase in Aramaic, the Targum, names the Servant of 52:13 as the Messiah. In 53:5 it reads the word for "pierced" as "profaned" and applies it to the sanctuary. The Hebrew letters allow both senses.

passages.saying: I am watching over My word to accomplish it.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Young Jeremiah protests, "I am only a child!" God touches his mouth, puts His words there, and sends him "to uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and plant." Then He asks, "Jeremiah, what do you see?"

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Jeremiah 1:12: the almond blossoms in January or February and is the harbinger of spring. Jamieson, Fausset and Brown: literally the wakeful tree, waking from winter's sleep before the others. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch note the play on the name.
layers.text: Jeremiah sees "a branch of an almond tree," shaqed, and God answers that He is shoqed, "watching." The almond is the first tree to blossom after winter, so its name means something like "the wakeful tree." God is awake over His word.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Amos 8:2: qets (end) sounds like qayits (summer fruit). Keil and Delitzsch on Amos 8:2: qets is chosen to form a paronomasia with qayits. Poole on Jeremiah 1:11 links the almond rod to Amos's summer fruit.
layers.text: Amos had a vision built the same way: "Amos, what do you see?" "A basket of summer fruit," qayits. Then God says the end, qets, "has come for My people Israel." Both visions turn an everyday object into a message through the sound of its name.

layers.evidence: Ellicott on Jeremiah 31:28 recalls the wakeful or watching tree. TAHOT: all three forms are H8245.
layers.text: The almond's verb returns beside the new-covenant promise: "Just as I watched over them to uproot and tear down," so "I will watch over them to build and to plant," the two tasks of Jeremiah's call. God watches over rebuilding as He watched over judgment.

layers.evidence: Ellicott, Barnes and Gill on Hebrews 8:8: the quotation in Hebrews 8:8-12 is from Jeremiah 31:31-34.
layers.text: Three verses later comes what He is watching to build, "a new covenant": "I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts." Hebrews quotes the whole passage and says of Jesus, "the covenant He mediates is better."

passages.saying: And this is His name by which He will be called: The LORD Our Righteousness.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Judah's rulers have been shepherds who "destroy and scatter the sheep of My pasture." God promises to "raise up for David a righteous Branch," a King who "will administer justice and righteousness in the land."

layers.evidence: TBESH H6667: Zedekiah, Jehovah is righteous, the last king of Judah, renamed from Mattaniah by Nebuchadnezzar. Ellicott: the reigning king's name implied the same thought, and his reign was a miserable failure.
layers.text: Judah's last king was Zedekiah, a name the king of Babylon gave him, meaning the LORD is righteous. Yet "Zedekiah did evil in the sight of the LORD." He bore a name close to the promised one and failed it; the true King will be "The LORD Our Righteousness."

layers.evidence: TBESH H6780: a sprout or shoot, used of the Messiah from David's tree. Keil and Delitzsch: tsemach denotes the Messiah. Poole ties it to the Branch of Jeremiah 33:15, and Ellicott to the Branch of Zechariah 3:8 and 6:12.
layers.text: "Branch" is tsemach, a sprout: the future King springing from David's family tree. Jeremiah repeats it, "I will cause to sprout for David a righteous Branch," and after the exile Zechariah hears, "I am going to bring My servant, the Branch."

layers.evidence: Ellicott on Jeremiah 23:6: in 33:16 the same name is given to Jerusalem. Gill and Jamieson, Fausset and Brown on 33:16: Christ and His church are one, so they share the name.
layers.text: When Jeremiah repeats the promise, the name moves from the King to His city: Jerusalem "will dwell securely, and this is the name by which it will be called: The LORD Our Righteousness." The King and His people share one name.

layers.evidence: Barnes and Poole see the King called Yahweh, and Poole links the name to 1 Corinthians 1:30. Keil and Delitzsch: he by whom Jahveh deals righteousness. Ellicott applies it to imputed righteousness.
layers.text: Christians have long read the name of Christ, whom Paul calls "our righteousness," in whom "we might become the righteousness of God." Some hear the King called the LORD Himself; others, the one through whom the LORD gives righteousness.

passages.saying: I saw One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven. He approached the Ancient of Days and was led into His presence.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT and TBESH, OpenBible.info cross-references, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Daniel sees four beasts rise from the sea, explained as "four kings who will arise from the earth." Then the Ancient of Days takes His throne, and one like a son of man comes with the clouds and is given an everlasting kingdom.

layers.evidence: TBESH: bar, son; enash, man, human being. Keil and Delitzsch: like a man, not a beast; clouds are the chariot on which God comes to judge (Psalm 104:3; Isaiah 19:1).
layers.text: In Aramaic "son of man" is bar enash, simply a human being. After the beasts comes a human figure, yet he arrives with "the clouds of heaven," and in Scripture clouds carry God Himself: "the LORD rides on a swift cloud." Human, and coming as God comes.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott on Daniel 7:14: in biblical Aramaic pelach is used only of the service and homage due to God. All 10 biblical uses are religious, though later Aramaic (Targum Onkelos) also uses it of farm work. Barnes on Daniel 7:14 compares Matthew 28:18.
layers.text: He is given a kingdom so "that the people of every nation and language should serve Him." The Bible uses this verb, pelach, only for religious service, as in "the God whom we serve." Jesus' last words echo the scene: all authority "has been given to Me."

layers.evidence: Gill on Mark 14:62, and Benson and Keil and Delitzsch on Daniel 7:13, tie Jesus' answer to this verse; His words also echo Psalm 110:1.
layers.text: Asked at His trial if He is the Christ, Jesus answers "I am," joining this verse to Psalm 110: "you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven." The high priest tears his clothes and cries blasphemy.

layers.evidence: TAGNT: the Son of Man occurs 80 times in the Gospels (NA28). TAHOT: ben adam occurs 94 times in Ezekiel; Ellicott: above ninety times. Matthew Henry's Concise: Christ usually called Himself the Son of man. Jamieson, Fausset and Brown: the title implies His lowliness and His exaltation.
layers.text: Son of Man was Jesus' favorite name for Himself, used about 80 times in the Gospels. It could sound humble: God calls Ezekiel "son of man" more than 90 times. But Jesus used it with authority: "the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins."

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch report some who read the figure as the people of Israel. Gill: the Messiah, as most Christian interpreters allow.
layers.text: The angel's explanation shares the kingdom: "the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom." Some medieval Jewish and modern commentators read the figure as Israel; most Christian interpreters see the Messiah, who shares His kingdom with His people.

layers.evidence: Gill, Barnes and Poole on Revelation 1:14: the description matches the Ancient of Days in Daniel 7:9.
layers.text: John sees "One like the Son of Man" whose hair is "white like wool, as white as snow," as Daniel described the Ancient of Days. The one who came to the throne shares the look of the One on it. And "He is coming with the clouds."

passages.saying: I will say to those called ‘Not My People,’ ‘You are My people,’ and they will say, ‘You are my God.’
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TBESH, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: God tells Hosea to marry an unfaithful wife, a living picture of Israel "departing from the LORD," and later to love her again, "as the LORD loves the Israelites, though they turn to other gods." Their children's names carry God's message.

layers.evidence: Benson, Barnes and Ellicott on Hosea 1:4: the massacre of Ahab's family by Jehu. Jamieson, Fausset and Brown and Ellicott: Jezreel sounds like Israel; NET Bible notes: yizre'el sounds like yisra'el. TBESH: Lo-ruhamah, no mercy; Lo-ammi, not my people.
layers.text: Each name is a sermon. Jezreel, which sounds like "Israel," recalls Jehu's massacre of Ahab's family there: "I will bring the bloodshed of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu." Lo-ruhamah means "no mercy," and Lo-ammi "not my people": "you are not My people."

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Hosea 1:9: the Hebrew reads lo' 'ehyeh lakhem, I will not be yours; an allusion to Exodus 3:12, 14 and in effect a negation of it. TAHOT: all three are H1961.
layers.text: Literally, 1:9 ends with God saying He will not be (ehyeh) theirs. Ehyeh is the word God spoke at the burning bush: "I will surely be with you" and "I AM WHO I AM." Hosea's line turns that promise around.

layers.evidence: TBESH H3157: Jezreel, God sows. Barnes: God changes the name's meaning to God shall sow. Jamieson, Fausset and Brown: no longer God will scatter but God will plant. Ellicott: the word sow alludes to and explains Jezreel.
layers.text: Then God turns the names inside out. Jezreel means "God sows," so the name of judgment becomes a harvest: the grain, wine and oil "will respond to Jezreel," and God says, "I will sow her as My own in the land." The God who scattered now plants.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch: salvation is announced by simply turning the names into their opposites, dropping the lo (not). TAHOT: ammi (H5971) and ruhamah (H7355) in 2:1 and 2:23.
layers.text: The other two names simply lose their "not": "Say of your brothers, ‘My people,’ and of your sisters, ‘My loved one,’" in Hebrew ammi and ruhamah. Where they were told "You are not My people," "they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’"

layers.evidence: TBESH H5911: Achor, the valley of trouble where Achan was stoned; H5916 akhar, to trouble. The Pulpit Commentary on Joshua 7:25: Joshua uses akhar for both Achan's sin and his punishment. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch on Hosea 2:15. NET Bible notes on Hosea 2:15.
layers.text: Even a place name is redeemed. The Valley of Achor, "trouble," was named for Achan's sin: "Why have you brought this trouble upon us?" Joshua asked. "Today the LORD will bring trouble upon you!" Now God will "make the Valley of Achor into a gateway of hope."

layers.evidence: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown and the Pulpit Commentary on Romans 9:25: first said of the ten tribes; the apostle legitimately applies it to the Gentiles. Ellicott: typically and prophetically applied to the Gentiles.
layers.text: Hosea spoke of the northern tribes coming back to God. Paul applies his words to those God called "not only from the Jews, but also from the Gentiles," and Peter tells his readers, "Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God."

passages.saying: Gilgal will surely go into exile, and Bethel will come to nothing.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.evidence: Amos 1:1 dates Amos to the days of Uzziah of Judah and Jeroboam of Israel. A few decades later Assyria captured Samaria and carried the Israelites away into exile (2 Kings 17:6).
layers.text: Amos speaks to the northern kingdom of Israel. Its people made trips to old holy places like Bethel and Gilgal while they "trample on the poor." God says, "Seek Me and live!" The shrines they trusted cannot save them; they too will fall.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: Gilgal (H1537) and galoh yigleh, it will surely go into exile (H1540, twice), in Amos 5:5. Gilgal and galah come from different roots, so the link is one of sound, not word history. Joshua 5:9 gives the Bible's own account of the name: there God rolled away (galal) the reproach of Egypt.
layers.text: In Hebrew the line is a run of matching sounds: ha-gilgal galoh yigleh, "Gilgal will surely go into exile." The name Gilgal and galah, the verb for going into exile, share the sounds g and l, so the town's name rings with its fate.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: Bet-el (H1008) and aven (H0205) in Amos 5:5; Bet aven (H1007) in Hosea 4:15, beside Gilgal, and 10:5. Joshua 7:2 names a real Beth-aven near Bethel, but Barnes, Jamieson, Fausset and Brown and the Pulpit Commentary take Hosea's Beth-aven, with its calf (Hosea 10:5), as a name for Bethel, where Jeroboam set up a golden calf (1 Kings 12:28-29).
layers.text: Bethel means "house of God." Amos says it "will come to nothing," and nothing is aven, a word for emptiness and wickedness. Many think Hosea made it a nickname: "do not go up to Beth-aven," house of wickedness, not house of God.

passages.saying: The end has come for My people Israel
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: God shows Amos a basket of ripe summer fruit and asks what he sees. The answer becomes the message: Israel's time is up. The next verses say why: they "trample the needy" and cheat the poor with dishonest scales.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: qayits (H7019) in 8:1 and 8:2, qets (H7093) in 8:2. Keil and Delitzsch and Gill note the paronomasia. Late summer fruit, such as figs, was the last crop of the farming year, which gives the picture its point; Barnes: when it was gathered, the circle of husbandry came to its close.
layers.text: Summer fruit is qayits; the end is qets. The two words sound almost alike, so the vision works like a spoken pun: Amos sees qayits and hears qets. Summer fruit was the last harvest of the year, and Israel's season is ending.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: qets (H7093) in Ezekiel 7:2 and 7:6; heqits, it has awakened (H6974), in 7:6. Ezekiel 7:2 repeats the words of Amos 8:2, the end has come, and speaks to the land of Israel, which by Ezekiel's day meant Judah. The Pulpit Commentary hears an echo of Amos and, with Keil and Delitzsch, notes the pun in 7:6.
layers.text: Over a century later Ezekiel brings the cry to "the land of Israel," which by then meant Judah: "The end! The end has come." He adds a pun of his own: the end (qets) "has roused itself" (heqits) against you. The end has woken up.

Jeremiah's first vision is built the same way: "Jeremiah, what do you see?" An almond branch, shaqed, and God is shoqed, "watching over My word." The prophets heard God's message in the names of ordinary things.

passages.saying: Forty more days and Nineveh will be overturned!
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: Jonah runs from God's call, is swallowed by a great fish, and finally preaches in Nineveh. The city repents and God spares it, to Jonah's anger.

layers.evidence: TBESH lists both senses of haphak. The Pulpit Commentary: the word used for the destruction of Sodom. BibleProject: it can also mean transformation, so Jonah's words came true, but not as he intended.

cites.at: BibleProject, Book of Jonah guide

layers.text: "Overturned" is haphak, the verb used when God overthrew Sodom (BSB "destroyed"). But it can also mean to be turned or changed. Nineveh was overturned, just not as Jonah expected: it turned around.

layers.evidence: Gary Yates (JETS 2016) notes Jonah goes down (yarad) in 1:3, 1:5 and 2:6, a downward descent of disobedience to the brink of Sheol.

cites.at: Gary Yates, The "Weeping Prophet" and "Pouting Prophet" in Dialogue, JETS 59/2 (2016)

layers.text: The story moves step by step downward: Jonah goes down to Joppa, down into the ship, down into its hold, and down to the roots of the mountains, the same verb (yarad) each time, until God raises his life from the pit.

layers.evidence: Name meaning from TBESH; Barnes and Jamieson, Fausset and Brown on Jonah 1:1: Jonah means dove. Maclaren: Jonah becomes a kind of representative of Israel.
layers.text: Jonah means "dove." Hosea calls the northern kingdom "a silly, senseless dove," and some readers see the runaway prophet as a picture of Israel itself.

Jesus names "the sign of the prophet Jonah": as Jonah was three days and three nights in the fish, so the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth. Nineveh repented, "and now One greater than Jonah is here."

Jonah sailed from Joppa to avoid preaching to Nineveh. Centuries later Peter, whom Jesus called "Simon son of Jonah" (John's Gospel has "son of John"), is staying in Joppa when God sends him to the Gentile Cornelius.

passages.saying: Roll in the dust in Beth-leaphrah.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: Micah came from Moresheth in Judah's foothills. He mourns the towns around his home one by one as disaster, most likely an invading army, sweeps through them toward Jerusalem: it "has approached the gate of my people, as far as Jerusalem itself."

layers.evidence: TAHOT: Beth-le'aphrah (H1036) and aphar, dust (H6083), in 1:10. TBESH gives the name as house belonging to Aphrah or house of dust. Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, Ellicott, Barnes and the Pulpit Commentary note the puns in Micah 1:10-15, though the sense of some is uncertain.
layers.text: Micah mourns town by town with puns on their names. Beth-leaphrah sounds like "house of dust," so its people must roll in the dust (aphar). English cannot keep these puns, and the sense of a few is uncertain, but the names echo the grief.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: Akhziv (H0392) and akhzav (H0391) in 1:14; Mareshah (H4762) and hayyoresh, the one who takes possession (H3423), in 1:15. Jeremiah 15:18 uses akhzav for a stream that fails, rendered mirage.
layers.text: The puns run on. "The houses of Achzib will prove deceptive": Achzib (akhziv) will be akhzav, the word Jeremiah uses for a stream that fails, "water that is not there." To Mareshah God will bring "a conqueror," ha-yoresh, which echoes its name.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: Micah 1:10 begat al-taggidu and 2 Samuel 1:20 al-taggidu begat use the same words, Gath (H1661) and tell (H5046), in reverse order. Some also hear a sound-play between gat and taggidu.
layers.text: Micah's lament for the towns opens, "Do not tell it in Gath," the words of David's lament for Saul and Jonathan: "Tell it not in Gath." Micah borrows David's famous funeral song to grieve for his own neighbors.

passages.saying: For Gaza will be abandoned
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: Zephaniah turns from Judah to its old enemies, the Philistine cities on the coastal plain, and announces that each will fall. Even this message ends with hope for Judah's remnant: "the LORD their God will attend to them."

layers.evidence: TAHOT: Azzah (H5804) with azuvah (H5800), and Eqron (H6138) with te'aqer (H6131), in the one verse. Keil and Delitzsch, the Pulpit Commentary and Gill point out both plays; Ashkelon and Ashdod have no clear pun.
layers.text: Two of the city names already sound like their fate. Gaza, azzah, will be azuvah, "abandoned," and Ekron, eqron, te'aqer, "uprooted." English loses it, but a Hebrew listener would hear the warning in the names themselves.

layers.evidence: Zechariah 9:5-7 names Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron and Ashdod, as Zephaniah does, and begins with judgment. The Jebusites held Jerusalem until David took it; afterward they lived on within Israel (1 Kings 9:20-21). Keil and Delitzsch, the Pulpit Commentary and Jamieson, Fausset and Brown read the comparison as Ekron being taken into God's people.
layers.text: A later prophet also foresees judgment on these cities, then goes further: God will cleanse them, "they too will become a remnant for our God," and "Ekron will be like the Jebusites," who stayed on and lived among Israel after David took their city.

passages.saying: Behold, I will send My messenger, who will prepare the way before Me.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT and TBESH, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, the Septuagint, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: The people complain, "Where is the God of justice?" God answers that He will send a messenger to clear the way, and then the Lord Himself will come to His temple, "like a refiner’s fire," to purify His people.

layers.evidence: TBESH H4401: Malachi, My messenger. JFB (Fausset) takes it as the name of an office, as the Septuagint of 1:1 (by the hand of his messenger) suggests; the Pulpit Commentary holds it is a proper name. Ellicott: the prophet chose the word with his own name in mind.
layers.text: The prophet's name, Malachi, means "My messenger," the very words of this verse. The word recurs: a priest "is the messenger of the LORD of Hosts." Some think Malachi is a title rather than a name; the Greek Old Testament of 1:1 has "his messenger."

layers.evidence: TBESH H4397: messenger, angel; TAHOT tags both messengers in 3:1 H4397. Ellicott: it must mean God Himself, since He comes to His temple; Jamieson, Fausset and Brown and the Pulpit Commentary agree.
layers.text: The verse has two messengers. The first prepares the way; the second, the "Messenger of the covenant," is "the Lord whom you seek" and comes "to His temple," His own house. Mal'akh means messenger or angel, and many read the second as God Himself arriving.

layers.evidence: Pulpit, Bengel and Ellicott on Matthew 11:10: Christ applies to Himself a prophecy of God's coming. The Septuagint of Exodus 23:20 and TAGNT of Matthew 11:10 share idou egō apostellō ton angelon mou pro prosōpou sou. NET Bible notes on Mark 1:2. TAHOT: in Hebrew both verses open with sholeach (sending) and mal'akh (messenger or angel).
layers.text: Jesus applies the verse to John the Baptist, changing "before Me" to "before You": the messenger prepares for God, and Jesus takes that place. Matthew's Greek matches Exodus 23:20, "I am sending an angel before you," and so do the Hebrew openings.

layers.evidence: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown on Malachi 4:5: an Elijah in spirit, not the literal Elijah. Keil and Delitzsch: Elijah was sent in the person of John. Barnes: in denying he was Elijah (John 1:21), John denied only that he was that great prophet himself.
layers.text: Malachi names the messenger: "I will send you Elijah the prophet." John would come "in the spirit and power of Elijah," and Jesus calls him "the Elijah who was to come." Yet asked "Are you Elijah?", John said, "I am not": the role returned, not the man.

layers.evidence: Matthew Henry and Keil and Delitzsch on Malachi 4:5: the close of Old Testament prophecy. Orthodox Bibles follow the Septuagint order and end the prophets with Daniel. NET Bible notes on Mark 1:2-3 and 1:6; Benson and Gill on 2 Kings 1:8: John dressed like Elijah.
layers.text: Malachi closes the Old Testament in Protestant and Catholic Bibles, and Mark opens by quoting it with Isaiah's "voice of one calling." Then John appears dressed like Elijah, "with a leather belt around his waist." The story resumes where the prophets left off.

layers.evidence: Bengel on Matthew 17:3 and Ellicott on Malachi 4:5: both are named together in Malachi 4:4-5. The Pulpit Commentary: they represent the Law and the Prophets.
layers.text: Malachi's closing lines name Moses and Elijah together: "Remember the law of My servant Moses" and "I will send you Elijah the prophet." On the mountain of transfiguration those two appear, "talking with Jesus," the Law and the Prophets gathered around Him.

passages.saying: you are Peter, and on this rock I will build My church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAGNT, TAHOT and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, Tertullian and John Chrysostom, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Near Caesarea Philippi Jesus asks, "Who do you say I am?" Simon Peter answers, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." Jesus says this was revealed to him by His Father in heaven, and promises to build His church.

layers.evidence: Tertullian (Prescription Against Heretics 22): Peter; John Chrysostom (Homilies on Matthew 54): the faith Peter confessed; Ellicott lists Peter's faith, the truth he confessed, or Christ. TBESG: petra is a mass of rock, petros a stone, but Ellicott notes the two Greek words differ in gender and were identical in Aramaic.
layers.text: Jesus puns on the name: "you are Peter, and on this rock I will build My church." In Matthew's Greek, Peter is Petros and rock is petra; a man's name takes the masculine form. What the rock is has long been debated: Peter, the faith he confessed, or Christ.
