layers.evidence: Ellicott: the two words were identical in the Aramaic Jesus probably spoke; the Pulpit Commentary gives the one word, kepha. TBESG: Cephas is the Aramaic kepha, Peter. The Syriac version, a later translation from the Greek, has kepha both times (Bengel). Not all agree: some read the change from petros to petra as meaningful.
layers.text: Jesus probably spoke Aramaic, and John keeps Peter's Aramaic name, Cephas, "which is translated as Peter"; Paul uses it too. Kepha means rock, so if Jesus said kepha both times, as Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary hold, the pun was exact: the same word twice.

layers.evidence: Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary link the keys to Eliakim in Isaiah 22:22, and Ellicott and Poole to Revelation 3:7. Barnes: to bind was to forbid, to loose to allow, a phrase often used by the Jews, as in the saying that the school of Shammai binds.
layers.text: Jesus gives Peter "the keys of the kingdom of heaven." Isaiah's steward Eliakim was given "the key to the house of David. What he opens no one can shut," and Revelation gives it to Jesus. Binding and loosing were rabbis' words for forbidding and allowing.

layers.evidence: Ellicott and Bengel find the phrase in Hezekiah's song (Isaiah 38:10); Gill cites Job 38:17, where the Septuagint has the same phrase. The NET Bible note: Hades is the Hebrew Sheol. TBESG: in the Greek Old Testament hades chiefly renders Sheol, and pyle (gate) renders sha'ar. The NET Bible note: the gates of Hades may stand for the power of death.
layers.text: "The gates of Hades" is Old Testament language. Facing death, Hezekiah says, "I must go through the gates of Sheol," and God asks Job, "Have the gates of death been revealed to you?" Hades is Greek for Sheol. Death will not overpower what Jesus builds.

layers.evidence: The Pulpit Commentary and Ellicott on John 1:42 compare the renamings of Abram, Sarai and Jacob.
layers.text: God renames people at turning points: Abram becomes Abraham, "a father of many nations," and Jacob becomes Israel. On first meeting Simon, Jesus does the same: "You will be called Cephas." Older commentators compare these renamings.

passages.saying: whom He named Boanerges
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: Jesus chose twelve men "to accompany Him, to be sent out to preach." Three of them received new names: Simon was named Peter, and the fishermen brothers James and John, sons of Zebedee, were named Boanerges.

layers.evidence: TAGNT: Boanerges (G0993) and brontes, of thunder (G1027). Abbott-Smith's lexicon (in TBESG) notes the derivation is debated. Ellicott: an Aramaic compound, b'ne regesh; Hammond, quoted by Benson, takes it as sons of commotion; Gill notes the odd form. Mark translates other Aramaic words the same way (5:41, 7:34).
layers.text: Boanerges is not a Greek word but most likely Aramaic, the language Jesus probably spoke. Mark keeps it and translates it: "Sons of Thunder." Boane- is usually taken as bene, "sons of"; the rest is harder to trace, and its derivation is still debated.

layers.evidence: Luke 9:51-56. Barnes and Ellicott tie the nickname to their fiery zeal, as in this scene; Benson and Gill suggest it honors their forceful preaching. The text itself does not say.
layers.text: The Gospels never say why Jesus gave the name. Many find it fits a later scene: when a Samaritan village turned Jesus away, James and John asked, "do You want us to call down fire from heaven to consume them?" Jesus rebuked them.

passages.saying: Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAGNT, TAHOT and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the Septuagint, the NET Bible notes, and Brandon Crowe's article in The Gospel Coalition.

layers.text: At night the disciples strain to row against the wind. In the fourth watch Jesus comes to them walking on the sea. They think He is a ghost and cry out, until He speaks, climbs into the boat, and the wind dies down.

layers.evidence: Brandon Crowe (The Gospel Coalition) hears Job 9 in Mark 6:48. The Septuagint of Job 9:8 has peripaton epi thalasses, walking on the sea, as Mark has peripaton epi tes thalasses.

cites.at: Brandon D. Crowe, To Understand Jesus Walking on Water, Read the Old Testament (The Gospel Coalition)

layers.text: In the Old Testament it is God who walks on the sea: "He alone stretches out the heavens and treads on the waves of the sea." The Greek Old Testament has Him walking on the sea, in the words Mark uses when Jesus comes "walking on the sea."

layers.evidence: Brandon Crowe (The Gospel Coalition) links Exodus 33, 1 Kings 19 and Job 9. The NET Bible note gives both readings and cites Exodus 33:19, 22. The Septuagint has parerchomai, Mark's verb, in all three passages.

cites.at: Brandon D. Crowe, To Understand Jesus Walking on Water, Read the Old Testament (The Gospel Coalition)

layers.text: "He intended to pass by them" recalls God passing by Moses and Elijah: "the LORD is about to pass by." Job says, "Were He to pass by me, I would not see Him." The Greek Old Testament uses Mark's verb in each. Others take it as how it looked to the disciples.

layers.evidence: Brandon Crowe (The Gospel Coalition): ego eimi could better be rendered I am, the language of the LORD's self-revelation. The Septuagint of Isaiah 43 has me phobou (do not fear) in verse 1, meta sou eimi in verse 2 and ego eimi in verse 10.

cites.at: Brandon D. Crowe, To Understand Jesus Walking on Water, Read the Old Testament (The Gospel Coalition)

layers.text: "It is I" is ego eimi, literally "I am." It can be ordinary speech (the healed man says it in John 9:9), but here it may echo Isaiah 43, which pairs the same words in Greek too: "Do not fear," "When you pass through the waters, I will be with you," "I am He."

layers.evidence: Brandon Crowe (Westminster Theological Seminary, writing in The Gospel Coalition): the miracle anticipates the Transfiguration in Mark 9:2-8.

cites.at: Brandon D. Crowe, To Understand Jesus Walking on Water, Read the Old Testament (The Gospel Coalition)

layers.text: The two men God "passed by" on His mountain were Moses and Elijah, and three chapters later they appear on another mountain, "talking with Jesus." One scholar reads the sea crossing as pointing ahead to that moment of glory.

layers.evidence: Brandon Crowe (The Gospel Coalition) reads it as a new exodus led by the incarnate I am, citing Psalm 77:16-20 and Isaiah 43:16.

cites.at: Brandon D. Crowe, To Understand Jesus Walking on Water, Read the Old Testament (The Gospel Coalition)

layers.text: Psalm 77 remembers the exodus: "Your path led through the sea, Your way through the mighty waters, but Your footprints were not to be found." Isaiah's LORD "makes a way in the sea." Some read the night crossing as a new exodus, led by the "I am" Himself.

passages.saying: The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: Jesus ends His parable of the tenants, who kill the owner's beloved son, by quoting Psalm 118. The leaders understand that He told the parable against them.
In the psalm the rejected stone becomes the head of the corner: "This is from the LORD, and it is marvelous in our eyes." The rejection is not the end; God reverses it.
Days earlier the crowds greeted Jesus with the same psalm: "Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!" The week opens with one verse of Psalm 118 and turns on another.
In Hebrew "son" is ben and "stone" is even (eben). Some scholars suggest the parable's rejected son and the psalm's rejected stone are tied by this sound.

In Luke, Jesus adds that whoever falls on this stone will be broken and whoever it falls on will be crushed, drawing on Isaiah's "stone of stumbling" and Daniel's stone, cut without hands, that crushes the kingdoms and fills the earth.

The apostles keep building with this stone: Peter quotes it to the rulers and elders in Jerusalem, calls believers "living stones," and joins it to Isaiah's precious cornerstone, and Paul names Christ the cornerstone.

passages.saying: This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAGNT, TAHOT, TBESG and TBESH, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, the Reformation Study Bible notes, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: At the Passover meal on His last night, Jesus breaks the bread, saying, "this is My body," then gives the cup: "This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many." He explains His death before it happens.

layers.evidence: Gill and Poole on Exodus 24:8 tie Moses' words to Christ's at the Supper, and Ellicott on Matthew 26:28 traces the phrase to Exodus 24:4-8. TBESG: diatheke nearly always renders berit in the Greek Old Testament.
layers.text: Jesus takes up Moses' words at Sinai. Moses sprinkled blood on the people and said, "This is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you." The first covenant was sealed in blood, and Hebrews quotes Moses' words as it explains the death of Christ.

layers.evidence: Gill on Exodus 24:11: a feast was common at covenant making; Keil and Delitzsch see the Sinai meal as a type of the marriage supper of the Lamb. On the parallel Matthew 26:29, Ellicott cites Isaiah 25:6 and the Pulpit Commentary reads it as the marriage supper of the Lamb.
layers.text: At Sinai the covenant ended in a meal: the elders "saw the God of Israel," and "they ate and drank." Jesus seals His covenant at a table too, and looks ahead to drinking "anew in the kingdom of God," at Isaiah's feast where God "will swallow up death forever."

layers.evidence: In Mark 14:24 the most reliable manuscripts lack new (kaines), which other copies likely took from Luke 22:20 (NET Bible note; TAGNT). The NET Bible note: Jesus' death established the forgiveness promised in Jeremiah 31:31. Ellicott on Matthew 26:28 points to Jeremiah 31:31-34.
layers.text: Luke and Paul record "the new covenant in My blood," and Matthew adds "for the forgiveness of sins." Jeremiah had promised a new covenant written on the heart: "I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more."

layers.evidence: The Reformation Study Bible note on Mark 14:24: Jesus alludes to Isaiah 53:12. Jeannine K. Brown (JETS 2020) finds allusions to Isaiah 53 in Mark 10:45 and 14:24; Maclaren on Isaiah 53:12 joins it to the ransom for many. The echo of poured out is with the Hebrew, he'erah (TAHOT; TBESH); the Greek Old Testament shares only many.

cites.at: Jeannine K. Brown, Jesus Messiah as Isaiah's Servant of the Lord, JETS 63.1 (2020)

layers.text: "Poured out for many" echoes Isaiah's suffering servant, who "poured out His life unto death" and "bore the sin of many." Jesus had already said He came "to give His life as a ransom for many."

layers.evidence: The Reformation Study Bible note on Mark 14:24 points to the Passover blood that protected Israel and the covenant blood of Exodus 24:8; the NET Bible note says Jesus is reinterpreting the Passover meal.
layers.text: It is Passover, "when the Passover lamb was to be sacrificed." In Egypt the lamb's blood on the doorframes shielded Israel: "when I see the blood, I will pass over you." At Sinai blood sealed the covenant. In this cup Jesus gathers both.

passages.saying: But when a Samaritan on a journey came upon him, he looked at him and had compassion.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, Strong's, Augustine's Tractates on John, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: An expert in the law, "wanting to justify himself," asks Jesus, "And who is my neighbor?" Jesus tells of a man beaten on the road down to Jericho. A priest and a Levite pass by; a Samaritan stops, binds his wounds and pays for his care. "Go and do likewise."

layers.evidence: Ellicott on Leviticus 19:34: the command to love your neighbor as yourself is here enacted for the stranger. Both verses use ve'ahavta (you shall love) and kamokha (as yourself) (TAHOT); a ger is a foreigner living in Israel (TBESH).
layers.text: The lawyer quotes Leviticus: "Love your neighbor as yourself," said there of "any of your people." Sixteen verses on it says of the foreigner living in Israel, "love him as yourself," in the same Hebrew. The law's love already reached past Israel's own people.

layers.evidence: Ellicott on 2 Chronicles 28:15: some have supposed our Lord had this passage in mind, and the likenesses between the two stories are curious. Gill: these men of Samaria acted the part of the good Samaritan.
layers.text: Some commentators hear an older story. In 2 Chronicles 28 men of Samaria, rebuked by a prophet, clothed their captives from Judah, "anointed their wounds, and put all the feeble on donkeys," and brought them to Jericho.

layers.evidence: Barnes on Luke 10:33: the Samaritans were the Jews' most inveterate foes, with no dealings between them (compare John 4:9). Gill: above all men hated by the Jews.
layers.text: Jews and Samaritans were bitter neighbors: "Jews do not associate with Samaritans." A chapter earlier a Samaritan village refused Jesus, and James and John wanted to "call down fire from heaven." Jesus rebuked them, then made a Samaritan the hero of His story.

layers.evidence: Strong's: to have the bowels yearn, to feel sympathy, to pity. TAGNT has it in 12 verses, all in the first three Gospels: 8 of Jesus, 1 in a plea to Him (Mark 9:22), and 3 in parables. Benson: the Samaritan's bowels yearned; Matthew Henry's Concise turns from his compassion to the compassion of Jesus.
layers.text: "Had compassion" is splanchnizomai, to be moved in one's inmost parts. The Gospels use it for Jesus, in a plea to Him, and in parables for the forgiving master, the father who runs to his lost son, and this Samaritan. The outsider feels what Jesus feels.

layers.evidence: Augustine, Tractates on John 43: Samaritan means keeper, and the Samaritan of the parable is our Keeper. TBESH: shamar, to keep or guard; Samaria, watch mountain.

cites.at: Augustine, Tractates on the Gospel of John 43.2

layers.text: Opponents once called Jesus "a Samaritan," and He denied only the demon. An early Christian reading took Samaritan to mean keeper (from shamar, to keep) and saw the Lord in the Samaritan: "The LORD is your keeper," who "will neither slumber nor sleep."

passages.saying: Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: Asked for a sign in the temple courts, Jesus answers with a riddle. His hearers take Him to mean the temple building, which had taken 46 years to build.

layers.evidence: Abbott-Smith's lexicon (in TBESG) cites this passage for both senses of egeiro
layers.text: John explains: "Jesus was speaking about the temple of His body." The verb egeiro means both to raise a building and to raise the dead. The disciples understood only after the resurrection.

The misunderstood saying returns as a charge at His trial and a taunt at the cross: "You who are going to destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days." The mockers are watching the first half come true.

layers.evidence: Abbott-Smith's lexicon (in TBESG): in the Greek Old Testament this verb chiefly stands for shakan
layers.text: John has said the Word "made His dwelling among us." The verb comes from the word for a tent, and in the Greek Old Testament it chiefly stands for shakan, the root of mishkan, the tabernacle where God's glory dwelt. Jesus' body is where God lives among His people.
The temple thread keeps widening: believers' bodies become "a temple of the Holy Spirit," and the new Jerusalem has no temple, "because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple."

passages.saying: Truly, truly, I tell you, no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Nicodemus, a Pharisee and a leader of the Jews, comes to Jesus at night. Jesus tells him that no one can see the kingdom of God without being born again, and Nicodemus asks how a grown man could enter his mother's womb a second time.

layers.evidence: NET Bible note: anothen means both again and from above, mainly from above here; Abbott-Smith (TBESG) reads again, as most do. In John, TAGNT has it only at 3:3, 3:7, 3:31, 19:11 and 19:23. Barnes: the language Jesus used probably lacked the Greek ambiguity. Ellicott: His word almost certainly had one sense, and the early Syriac version reads anew.
layers.text: In John's Greek, "born again" is anothen, which also means "from above," as in "The One who comes from above." Nicodemus hears only a second birth. Jesus likely spoke Aramaic, and many think His word had one sense, so the play on both may be John's.

layers.evidence: The NET Bible note on John 3:8 points out the wordplay on wind and spirit. TBESG: pneuma is wind, breath or spirit. TBESH: Aramaic ruach (rucha with the article) is wind or spirit; TAHOT has it as wind in Daniel 2:35 and 7:2 and as spirit in Daniel 5:12 and 7:15.
layers.text: "The wind blows where it wishes," and "So it is with everyone born of the Spirit." Wind and Spirit are one word in John's Greek, pneuma, and in Aramaic, rucha, so the saying works just as well in the language Jesus likely spoke.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown points to Ezekiel's promise of clean water and God's Spirit (Ezekiel 36:25-27). On the water, Barnes and Bengel see baptism, Poole the Spirit's cleansing of the soul, and Gill a figure of God's grace.
layers.text: "Born of water and the Spirit" joins two promises God made through Ezekiel: "I will also sprinkle clean water on you" and "I will put My Spirit within you." So Jesus expects Israel's teacher to understand. Commentators still differ on what the water means.

layers.evidence: The NET Bible note on John 3:5 points to Ezekiel 37:9-10. TBESH: ruach is wind, breath, mind or spirit; TAHOT has it four times in Ezekiel 37:9.
layers.text: Hebrew has the same double word, ruach. In Ezekiel's valley of dry bones it is breath, wind and Spirit at once: "Come from the four winds, O breath," and "I will put My Spirit in you and you will live."

layers.evidence: Ellicott on John 3:2: the night visit is recalled in the description of Nicodemus at 19:39. Matthew Henry: though he came by night, afterward he owned Christ publicly. Some, after Augustine, read the night as a symbol of his darkness; the Pulpit Commentary calls that far-fetched.
layers.text: Nicodemus came "at night," and John recalls it when he brings about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes for Jesus' burial. The man who first came to Jesus by night later honors Him openly.

passages.saying: Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up,
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: Jesus tells Nicodemus that, like the bronze snake Moses raised in the wilderness, He must be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in Him may have eternal life.
In Numbers the people speak against God, venomous snakes bite them, and God tells Moses to make a snake and set it on a pole. Moses makes it of bronze, and whoever is bitten and looks at it lives.

layers.evidence: Adam Clarke on Numbers 21:9: the word for brass comes from the same root as nachash, serpent. Ellicott on 2 Kings 18:4 hears both words in the name Nehushtan.
layers.text: In Hebrew, snake is nachash and bronze is nechoshet, so the "bronze snake" is a nechash nechoshet: the two words sound almost alike.

layers.evidence: TBESG (Abbott-Smith): hypsoo is to lift up (John 3:14, 12:32) and to exalt (Acts 2:33). The Aramaic behind it is debated; some propose a pun on zeqaph, used of a man lifted onto a beam in Ezra 6:11 (TAHOT).
layers.text: In John's Greek, "lifted up" (hypsoo) means raised up and also exalted. When Jesus says it again, John adds that it showed "the kind of death He was going to die," and Acts uses the verb for His exaltation to God's right hand. The cross is His lifting up.

layers.evidence: Ellicott on Isaiah 52:13: the phrase impressed itself, through the Greek Old Testament, on Christ's mind in reference to His crucifixion, citing John 3:14, 8:28 and 12:32.
layers.text: Isaiah's suffering servant "will be raised and lifted up and highly exalted," just before the description of His suffering. The Greek Old Testament uses the same verb there, and many scholars think John's "lifted up" draws on this verse.

layers.evidence: Meaning of nechoshet from TBESH
layers.text: Centuries later Israel was burning incense to that same bronze snake, now called Nehushtan, a name built on nechoshet, "bronze," and King Hezekiah smashed it. The sign had become an idol; the healing never lay in the bronze.

passages.saying: you would have asked Him, and He would have given you living water.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, the Mishnah, older commentaries named under each note, and an article by Carissa Quinn (BibleProject).

layers.text: Weary from His journey, Jesus sits by Jacob's well in Samaria and asks a Samaritan woman for a drink. She asks how a Jew can ask her. He offers her living water instead, "a fount of water springing up to eternal life."

layers.evidence: NET Bible note: the word translated living is used in Greek of flowing water. Abbott-Smith (TBESG): springing as opposed to still water. Barnes and Benson: living water meant spring or running water.
layers.text: In Greek, "living water" meant flowing water, from a spring rather than a cistern. So she asks how He will draw it, since "the well is deep." She hears spring water; Jesus means water that wells up to eternal life.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: mayim chayyim in Genesis 26:19 and Jeremiah 2:13, and the same chayyim in the cleansing law of Leviticus 14:5 (BSB fresh water there too). TBESH: chay is living, and of water, flowing or fresh. The Pulpit Commentary on John 4:10 cites Genesis 26:19 and Jeremiah 2:13.
layers.text: Hebrew says the same, mayim chayyim. Isaac's servants find "a well of fresh water" (literally living water), and Jeremiah gives the phrase to God: "They have forsaken Me, the fountain of living water, and they have dug their own cisterns."

layers.evidence: Carissa Quinn (BibleProject): when the biblical authors portray a man meeting his future bride, the setting is often a well (Rebekah, Rachel, Zipporah); calling it Jacob's well links the scene with Jacob and Rachel, and Jesus is called the groom in the chapter before.

cites.at: Carissa Quinn, BibleProject, 'Woman at the Well: What Jesus' Offer of Living Water Means' (2020)

layers.text: A man meets a woman at a well, and a marriage follows: Abraham's servant finds Rebekah, Jacob meets Rachel, Moses meets Zipporah. This is "Jacob’s well," a chapter after John the Baptist calls Jesus "the bridegroom." This time many in her town believe.

layers.evidence: Mishnah Sukkah 4:9 describes water drawn from the Siloam pool in a golden jug and poured at the altar. The NET Bible note on John 7:38: Jesus takes up the water of the ceremony and uses it figuratively.
layers.text: At the Feast of Tabernacles, when by Jewish tradition water from Siloam was poured at the altar, Jesus promises "streams of living water," meaning the Spirit. Zechariah's vision of living water from Jerusalem ends with the nations keeping that feast.

layers.evidence: NET Bible note: a question opened with me in Greek expects the answer no; Ellicott renders it "Thou surely art not greater." Bengel compares John 8:53; the Pulpit Commentary finds her words possibly ironic.
layers.text: She asks, "Are You greater than our father Jacob, who gave us this well?" In Greek the question expects the answer no, but John's readers know better. Jesus meets the same question about Abraham, and the Samaritans end up calling Him "the Savior of the world."

passages.saying: I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: The day after feeding five thousand, Jesus tells the crowd that He Himself is the bread that satisfies: whoever comes to Him will never hunger.

The crowd asks for a sign like the manna and quotes Scripture: "He gave them bread from heaven to eat," words close to Exodus 16:4 and Psalm 78:24. Jesus answers that the true bread from heaven comes from His Father, and unlike the manna, whoever eats it will not die.
Manna is named after a question. When Israel first saw it they asked one another, "What is it?" (man hu), and they called it man. Moses answered, "It is the bread that the LORD has given you to eat."

Moses said the manna taught Israel that "man does not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD." Jesus quotes this in the wilderness, and in John the Word made flesh is Himself the bread.
John notes that Passover was near. The bread Jesus will give "for the life of the world" is His flesh, which many readers connect with the Last Supper: "This is My body, given for you."

layers.evidence: Name meaning from TBESH
layers.text: Jesus was born in Bethlehem, whose name means "house of bread," and was laid in a manger, a feeding trough. Christians have long noticed the Bread of Life coming from the House of Bread; the Gospels do not point it out.

passages.saying: Go, wash in the Pool of Siloam
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, the Mishnah, Irenaeus and Augustine, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Jesus sees a man blind from birth. His disciples ask whose sin caused it; Jesus says neither: it happened "so that the works of God would be displayed in him." He makes mud, puts it on the man's eyes and sends him to wash. He comes back seeing.

layers.evidence: NET Bible note: the Hebrew name shiloah comes from the verb to send. Augustine, Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary see Jesus as the one Sent; Gill reports that reading, and Barnes doubts a link to Shiloh. John's word for Sent is a form of apostello, the verb of John 17:3 and 20:21 (TAGNT).
layers.text: John stops to translate the pool's name: Siloam, Isaiah's "Shiloah," means "Sent." In John, Jesus is the Sent One, doing "the works of Him who sent Me." So a man sent to the pool called Sent is healed by the One sent from God.

layers.evidence: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.15.2: the clay points to how man was first fashioned and shows the hand of God that formed him from the dust. The Greek pelos (clay) occurs in the New Testament only in John 9 and Romans 9:21 (TAGNT).

cites.at: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.15.2

layers.text: Only here in the Gospels does Jesus make mud to heal. An early Christian reading sees the Creator's hand: as God formed man "from the dust of the ground," so Jesus used clay on the eyes, showing how humanity was first made. John himself does not say this.

layers.evidence: The Pulpit Commentary on Isaiah 42:7: the Messiah would cure blindness of body and of spirit. Gill and the Pulpit Commentary on Matthew 11:5 hear the prophets' promises in Jesus' answer. Isaiah 35:5 and 42:7 share the verb paqach (open) and the noun ivver (blind) (TAHOT).
layers.text: "Never before has anyone heard of opening the eyes of a man born blind." Yet Isaiah promised that "the eyes of the blind will be opened," and that God's servant would open them. Asked by John the Baptist, Jesus points to such signs: "The blind receive sight."

layers.evidence: Gill on John 9:39 cites Isaiah 6:9, which John quotes in 12:40, and Ellicott points ahead to John 12:37-50. The NET Bible note calls the man's worship the climax of the story.
layers.text: The sign becomes a two-edged saying: "so that the blind may see and those who see may become blind." The man goes from "The man they call Jesus" to "a prophet" to worship, while leaders who "claim you can see" stay blind. John later ties this to Isaiah.

layers.evidence: Mishnah Sukkah 4:9 (water from Siloam poured at the altar) and 5:3 (every courtyard in Jerusalem lit), written down later. Ellicott and Gill on John 9:7 link Siloam's water to the feast; Ellicott and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on John 8:12 describe its great lamps.
layers.text: This follows the Feast of Tabernacles, where Jesus said, "I am the light of the world." Later Jewish writings say that feast drew water from Siloam for the altar and lit every courtyard in Jerusalem. Now the Light of the world sends a blind man there.

passages.saying: Lazarus, come out!
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, Genesis Rabbah, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: When His friend Lazarus falls sick, Jesus waits two days, saying the sickness is "for the glory of God." He arrives when Lazarus has been four days in the tomb, tells Martha, "I am the resurrection and the life," and calls the dead man out.

layers.evidence: Abbott-Smith (TBESG): a colloquial short form of Eleazar; TBESH: Eleazar means God has helped. Gill and the Pulpit Commentary on Luke 16:20 derive it from Eleazar; Ellicott and Barnes think the name may picture the beggar's helplessness.
layers.text: Lazarus is a short form of Eleazar, a Hebrew name meaning "God has helped." John never comments on the name. For Luke's beggar, some commentators think it may picture a man who had no other help; others see no symbolism.

layers.evidence: Bengel, Ellicott and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on Luke 16:31 note the match with the raising of Lazarus.
layers.text: In a parable in Luke, Jesus names a beggar Lazarus, and the story ends, "they will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead." In John a man named Lazarus rises, and the chief priests plan "to kill Lazarus as well." The Gospels never link the two.

layers.evidence: NET Bible note: Caiaphas meant political expediency, and John reads his words in a sense Caiaphas could not have imagined.
layers.text: Caiaphas argues, "it is better for you that one man die for the people." He means politics, but John says that as high priest he "was prophesying" that Jesus would die for the nation and for "the scattered children of God." One sentence, two meanings.

layers.evidence: Ellicott and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on John 11:43 point to John 5:25 and 5:28-29. The same noun, phone (voice), is in John 11:43 and 5:28 (TAGNT).
layers.text: Jesus had said that "all who are in their graves will hear His voice" and come out. At Bethany one grave hears that voice early: "The man who had been dead came out." It is a near, partial fulfillment of a far promise.

layers.evidence: Genesis Rabbah 100:7; Gill and the Pulpit Commentary on John 11:39 cite the tradition. Barnes: the four days rule out deception or a mere swoon.
layers.text: John mentions the four days twice, and Martha warns, "by now he stinks." A rabbinic saying, written down later, held that the soul stays near the grave for three days. After four days, commentators note, no one could say Lazarus had only seemed dead.

passages.saying: God raised Him from the dead, releasing Him from the agony of death, because it was impossible for Him to be held in its clutches.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the Septuagint, the NET Bible notes, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: At Pentecost Peter tells the crowd that Jesus died "by God’s set plan and foreknowledge," but God raised Him. Death had seized Him but could not keep Him: "it was impossible for Him to be held in its clutches."

layers.evidence: Ellicott: literally travail-pangs, from a Greek rendering of the Hebrew for cords of death. TBESH lists chevel, a cord, and chevel, pain or travail; Gill: the word signifies both cords and sorrows. The Septuagint of Psalm 18:4 has odines thanatou, as in Acts 2:24.
layers.text: The word behind "agony" is odines, labor pains. It echoes the Psalms: "The cords of death encompassed me." In Hebrew chevel means a cord, and a word with the same letters means a labor pain. The Greek Old Testament took it the second way, in Luke's very words.

layers.evidence: The Pulpit Commentary and Gill: loosed applies better to cords than to pangs. Ellicott reads the resurrection as a new birth from the womb of the grave. The Septuagint of Psalm 18:5 renders the cords of Sheol as odines hadou.
layers.text: Both senses fit. The verb for "releasing" is lyo, to untie, which suits cords better than pains: God loosed "the cords of Sheol." Some also hear a birth: death went into labor and could not hold what it bore.

layers.evidence: The Pulpit Commentary on Colossians 1:18, citing Acts 2:24: He comes out from the dead as the firstborn from the womb. Ellicott calls the resurrection His second birth, and Poole a kind of new birth. Barnes reads firstborn as rank, and TBESG files it under priority.
layers.text: Many hear the same picture in a title Paul and John both give Jesus: "firstborn from among the dead" and "the firstborn from the dead." Older commentators call the resurrection His second birth, coming out of the grave as a child comes from the womb.

layers.evidence: Ellicott on John 16:21: the figure was often used by the prophets (Isaiah 21:3, 26:17-18, 66:7-8). Isaiah 26:17 has chevel, pain (TAHOT); in 26:19 the verb for bring forth can mean give birth (NET Bible note).
layers.text: Jesus pictured the grief of His death and the joy of Easter as childbirth: the mother "forgets her anguish," and "I will see you again." Isaiah 26 uses the same picture: labor pains give way to "Your dead will live" and "the earth will bring forth her dead."

passages.saying: Do you understand what you are reading?
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: An Ethiopian official, treasurer to his queen, is riding home from worship in Jerusalem, reading Isaiah aloud. Philip runs up beside the chariot. The passage is about one "led like a sheep to the slaughter," and Philip tells him about Jesus.

layers.evidence: TAGNT: ginoskeis (G1097) and anaginoskeis (G0314) side by side. Abbott-Smith's lexicon (in TBESG) gives know again as the first sense of anaginosko and lists Acts 8:30 under read. Philip and the official may well have spoken Greek, but the wording we have is Luke's.
layers.text: In Luke's Greek, Philip's question is a pun: ginoskeis ha anaginoskeis? Ginosko means "to know," and the verb for read is the same word with ana- in front, "to know again." Reading the words is not yet knowing what they mean.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: sarisim, eunuchs (H5631), in Isaiah 56:4; TAGNT: eunouchos (G2135) in Acts 8:27. Ellicott, Barnes and Poole note that eunouchos may be only an official's title. Ellicott, Poole and Gill link the scene with Isaiah 56:3-5.
layers.text: Luke calls the reader a eunuch, a castrated man; the law kept such men out of the assembly. Soon after the passage he was reading, Isaiah promises faithful eunuchs "a memorial and a name better than that of sons and daughters." Many see that promise come true here.

passages.saying: they drank from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: Paul warns the Corinthians not to presume on their privileges: Israel was rescued, fed and given water in the wilderness, and still most of them fell.
Twice God gave water from a rock. At Horeb Moses was told to strike it; years later he was told to speak to it, struck it twice instead, and was barred from the land.

Moses named the place Massah (testing) and Meribah (quarreling) because the people asked, "Is the LORD among us or not?" Psalm 95 keeps the names as a warning, and Hebrews, quoting the psalm in Greek, gives their meanings: "in the rebellion, in the day of testing."

In the Song of Moses, Rock is a name for God: "He is the Rock, His work is perfect." Paul echoes that song twice in this chapter (sacrifices to demons, provoking God to jealousy), so "that rock was Christ" puts Christ in the place of Israel's God.
Paul names his way of reading: these things happened "as examples" and "were written down as warnings for us." The Greek words are typoi and typikos, where the word "type" comes from.
Jesus calls out, "If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink." Some readers also connect the struck rock with Christ pierced on the cross, when "blood and water flowed out" from His side.

passages.saying: Death has been swallowed up in victory.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the Septuagint, the NET Bible notes, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Paul ends his chapter on the resurrection with a mystery: "We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed." At the last trumpet the dead will rise imperishable, and then the saying will come true: "Death has been swallowed up in victory."

layers.evidence: NET Bible note on Isaiah 25:8: in Canaanite thought death was a hungry enemy swallowing its victims. The Pulpit Commentary calls Paul's words a free citation from the Hebrew; Bengel gives the Septuagint's wording, in which death prevails and swallows. TBESG: katapino renders bala.
layers.text: Paul quotes Isaiah's promise of a banquet "for all the peoples," where "He will swallow up death forever." Death was pictured as a hungry enemy swallowing its victims; here God swallows death. The common Greek version reversed it, so Paul follows the Hebrew.

layers.evidence: Barnes and Keil and Delitzsch on Isaiah 25:8: a kindred Aramaic (Chaldee) verb means to conquer, so the word may denote victory; Barnes adds that the Syriac unites victory and perpetuity. TBESG lists Septuagint renderings of netsach as eis nikos, including 2 Samuel 2:26.
layers.text: Isaiah's "forever" is netsach, which in Hebrew means perpetuity. A related Aramaic word means victory, so Greek translators often wrote "to victory," even in "Must the sword devour forever?" With that echo, one word holds both promises: forever, and victory.

layers.evidence: Readers differ. Gill and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown read a promise that God will not go back on; Ellicott reports that reading but prefers to hear death summoned against Ephraim, and the Pulpit Commentary sets out both. Where the Septuagint of Hosea has dike (penalty), Paul has nikos, victory (TBESG).
layers.text: Paul echoes Hosea: "Where, O Death, are your plagues? Where, O Sheol, is your sting?" Readers differ on Hosea's tone: a promise of rescue, or God calling death against Israel, for the verse ends "Compassion is hidden from My eyes." Paul makes it a taunt.

layers.evidence: Barnes and the Pulpit Commentary on Isaiah 25:8 point ahead to Revelation 21:4, and Ellicott to Revelation 7:17, which repeats the promise.
layers.text: Isaiah's verse goes on: "The Lord GOD will wipe away the tears from every face." Paul takes the first half and John the second: "He will wipe away every tear from their eyes," and "there will be no more death." One promise ends both death and tears.

layers.evidence: TBESG: katapino is the Septuagint's usual word for bala, swallow, as in Isaiah 25:8. Ellicott and Barnes on 2 Corinthians 5:4 compare 1 Corinthians 15:54.
layers.text: Paul uses the picture again: in this tent we groan, longing to be clothed, "so that our mortality may be swallowed up by life." The Greek verb is the same, katapino. Death used to do the swallowing. Now life does.

passages.saying: If anyone does not love the Lord, let him be under a curse. Come, O Lord!
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, the Didache (Lightfoot's translation), articles by David Capes and Michael Bird, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The Greek text spells out the Aramaic marana tha (NET Bible note).
layers.text: Paul takes the pen to write the closing greeting in his own hand. Then come a warning and a prayer: "If anyone does not love the Lord, let him be under a curse. Come, O Lord!" The prayer is in Aramaic, not Greek: marana tha.

layers.evidence: The NET Bible note gives both readings; David Capes: an acclamation, Our Lord comes, or an invocation, Come, our Lord. TAGNT: NA28, NA27 and SBL print marana tha; Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, the Textus Receptus and the Byzantine text print maran atha.

cites.at: David B. Capes, 'One God, One Lord (Part 8)' (2020)

layers.text: The Aramaic divides two ways. Marana tha (Our Lord, come!) is a prayer; maran atha (our Lord has come, or is coming) is a confession. Printed Greek texts divide it both ways. Both are true of Jesus: He came, and He is coming.

layers.evidence: Ellicott and Barnes call the words Syriac. David Capes: Qumran texts show the Aramaic Mareh (TBESH mare') could be a divine title, as Larry Hurtado argued. Michael Bird: the earliest churches of Judea and Syria called Jesus Lord in Aramaic and made Him the object of prayer in worship.

cites.at: Michael F. Bird, 'Maranatha and the Identity of Jesus', Word from the Bird (2024)
David B. Capes, 'One God, One Lord (Part 8)' (2020)

layers.text: Why Aramaic in a letter to Greeks? No one knows for sure, but many scholars hear a prayer of the first church in Judea, which called Jesus maran, our Lord, a title that could also be used of God. In their worship, Jesus was the one they prayed to.

layers.evidence: Didache 10.6, in J. B. Lightfoot's translation; New Advent's reads: Let grace come, and let this world pass away, and later Maran atha. Michael Bird notes the same language in Revelation and the Didache and reads the prayer as looking to Jesus' return.

cites.at: Didache 10.6
Michael F. Bird, 'Maranatha and the Identity of Jesus', Word from the Bird (2024)

layers.text: The Didache, an early Christian writing, ends its prayer after the Lord's Supper the same way, asking for grace to come and this world to pass away, then maran atha. Paul ties the Supper to the same hope: "you proclaim the Lord’s death until He comes."

layers.evidence: David Capes and Michael Bird compare Revelation 22:20. Barnes: John answers in the precise language the Savior had used.

cites.at: David B. Capes, 'One God, One Lord (Part 8)' (2020)
Michael F. Bird, 'Maranatha and the Identity of Jesus', Word from the Bird (2024)

layers.text: If Paul's words are the prayer marana tha, the Bible's last book closes with the same prayer in Greek. Jesus says, "Yes, I am coming soon," and John answers in His own words, "Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!" Both ask the Lord to come.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on Galatians 4:6: Christ's own cry becomes the believers' cry. TBESG: abba is Aramaic for father.
layers.text: Paul's Greek letters keep another Aramaic prayer word, Abba. Jesus prayed "Abba, Father" in Gethsemane, and the Spirit of the Son in our hearts cries "Abba, Father!" The Son's own cry becomes the cry of God's children.

passages.saying: we, who with unveiled faces all reflect the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into His image
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the Septuagint, the NET Bible notes, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Paul compares two ministries. At Sinai the Israelites "could not gaze at the face of Moses," and he veiled it. In Christ the veil is gone: believers "with unveiled faces" reflect the Lord's glory and are being changed into His image.

layers.evidence: Barnes: Moses has not himself declared the design of the veil; Ellicott, Bengel and the Pulpit Commentary say Paul gives the account his own turn. The Hebrew for this veil, masveh, occurs only in Exodus 34:33-35 (TAHOT).
layers.text: Paul is retelling Exodus 34. Moses came down Sinai "unaware that his face had become radiant," and after speaking to the people "he put a veil over his face." Exodus never says the glow faded; that detail is Paul's own reading.

layers.evidence: NET Bible note: qaran comes from qeren in the sense of a ray of light; Aquila's Greek and the Vulgate give horns. The Pulpit Commentary: the Hebrew words for a ray and a horn are identical. Gill: the Septuagint says his face was glorified. Barnes and Ellicott: the Latin rendering led painters to give Moses horns.
layers.text: The word for "radiant," qaran, comes from qeren, a horn or a ray (Habakkuk 3:4). The Greek Old Testament says his face was glorified, and Paul calls it glory. The Latin Bible said horned, and Michelangelo's Moses has horns, though the history is complex.

layers.evidence: Bengel calls the verse a paraphrase on Exodus 34:34, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown hears the same allusion. The Septuagint of Exodus 34:34 and Paul's verse share henika (whenever), periaireo (remove) and kalymma (veil).
layers.text: Exodus says that whenever Moses went in before the LORD, "he would remove the veil." Paul reworks it, keeping its Greek words for whenever, remove and veil: "whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away." What Moses alone did, anyone may now do.

layers.evidence: Ellicott and MacLaren: the same verb as the Transfiguration. It occurs only in Matthew 17:2, Mark 9:2, Romans 12:2 and here (TAGNT; TBESG).
layers.text: The word for "transformed" is metamorphoo, used when Jesus "was transfigured" and "His face shone like the sun." Its only other use is "be transformed by the renewing of your mind." Moses' face shone, Jesus' face shone, and now believers are being changed.

layers.evidence: TBESG: to reflect as a mirror; TAGNT: beholding as in a mirror. Barnes and the Pulpit Commentary read beholding; Ellicott and MacLaren weigh both senses of the verb.
layers.text: The verb for "reflect," katoptrizomai, comes from the word for a mirror. It can mean to reflect like a mirror or to look as into a mirror, and commentators split between the two. Moses did both: he met the LORD face to face, and his face shone.

layers.evidence: Ellicott and Gill hear the creation of light (Genesis 1:3) in these words; Ellicott and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown link the face of Jesus to the face of Moses.
layers.text: Paul goes back to creation: the God who said "Let light shine out of darkness" now gives "the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ." The face that shone at Sinai pointed to this face: Christ, "the image of God."

passages.saying: at the name of Jesus every knee should bow
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the Septuagint, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: To teach humility, Paul tells Christ's story. Existing "in the form of God," He "emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant," and became obedient to death on a cross. So God gave Him "the name above all names," before which every knee will bow.

layers.evidence: Barnes, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Pulpit Commentary hear Isaiah 45:23, which the Pulpit Commentary notes are the words of Jehovah.
layers.text: Paul's words come from Isaiah 45, where the LORD swears by Himself: "Every knee will bow before Me, every tongue will swear allegiance." He has just said, "I am God, and there is no other." Paul applies the LORD's own oath to Jesus.

layers.evidence: TBESG: kampto (bow) and exomologeo (confess) in Romans 14:11 and Philippians 2:10-11, from the Septuagint of Isaiah 45:23, whose printed editions vary between confess and swear. Barnes, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Pulpit Commentary note Romans 14:11.
layers.text: In Romans Paul quotes the same verse about God's judgment: "every knee will bow before Me; every tongue will confess to God." In Philippians the same bowing and confessing, in the same Greek verbs, happen at the name of Jesus, "to the glory of God the Father."

layers.evidence: TBESG: kyrios chiefly renders YHWH in the Septuagint. Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary (Lord, or Jehovah) read God's own name; MacLaren and Benson take it as the name Jesus, and Gill and Bengel as His dignity.
layers.text: Which is "the name above all names"? Many older commentators answer: Lord, the word the Greek Old Testament uses for God's own name, YHWH. Others disagree. Isaiah's speaker is "I, the LORD," and now every tongue confesses "that Jesus Christ is Lord."

layers.evidence: Ellicott: the Lord in Joel means Jehovah, and here it is applied to our Lord; Barnes, Poole and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown also apply it to Christ.
layers.text: Paul does the same with Joel. Joel's promise, "everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved," uses God's own name, YHWH. Romans quotes it soon after "if you confess with your mouth" that "Jesus is Lord," so the Lord to call on is Jesus.

layers.evidence: The Pulpit Commentary: Isaiah prophesied of Christ as the Servant of Jehovah (Isaiah 49 and 52). Gill: He was often prophesied of as a servant (Isaiah 42:1).
layers.text: The story follows Isaiah's suffering Servant. Christ takes "the form of a servant," is "obedient to death," and God exalts Him to the highest place. The Servant "will be raised and lifted up and highly exalted," because "He has poured out His life unto death."

layers.evidence: Matthew Poole and Gill contrast the sin of Adam and Eve; Bengel cites Genesis 3:5. Harpagmos (grasped) comes from harpazo, to seize, and its exact sense is disputed (TBESG).
layers.text: Some readers also hear Adam. The serpent promised, "you will be like God," and our first parents reached for it. Christ, though "in the form of God," "did not consider equality with God something to be grasped." It is an echo, not a quotation.

passages.saying: those mutilators of the flesh
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.evidence: "Dogs" was a sharp insult. Ellicott, Benson, Gill and the Pulpit Commentary say Paul turns back on these teachers a word Jews used for Gentiles, though the text does not say so. His target is these teachers and their teaching, not the Jewish people; he was a Jew himself.
layers.text: Paul warns the church, in harsh words, against teachers who most likely insisted that non-Jewish believers be circumcised to belong to God's people. Paul was himself a Jew, "circumcised on the eighth day"; he objects to making it a requirement.

layers.evidence: TAGNT: katatomen (G2699) in 3:2, peritome (G4061) in 3:3. Abbott-Smith's lexicon (in TBESG) says katatome is used here in sarcasm, by paronomasia (wordplay), in contrast to true peritome. Katatome occurs nowhere else in the New Testament.
layers.text: Paul's Greek has a sharp pun. Circumcision is peritome, "a cutting around." He calls these teachers the katatome, "a cutting up," in English "mutilators of the flesh." Then: "it is we who are the circumcision," meaning all who trust Christ, Jew or Gentile.
The idea of an inner circumcision is older than Paul. Moses promised, "The LORD your God will circumcise your hearts," and Paul writes that "circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit."

passages.saying: Formerly he was useless to you, but now he has become useful both to you and to me.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.evidence: Readers differ on what Paul is asking: that Philemon free Onesimus (Paul expects him to "do even more than I ask," Philemon 1:21), or that he welcome him as a brother while he stays a slave. The letter does not say. In later centuries both defenders and opponents of slavery appealed to it.

cites.at: Reformation Study Bible note on Philemon 1:11 (Bible Gateway)

layers.text: Onesimus, a slave, had left his master Philemon, a Christian, and met Paul while Paul was in prison; there he came to faith. Paul sends him back, asking Philemon to receive him "no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother."

layers.evidence: TAGNT: Onesimos (G3682) in 1:10; achreston (G0890) and euchreston (G2173) in 1:11. Abbott-Smith's lexicon (in TBESG): Onesimus means profitable, from onesis, profit, and was a common name among slaves. Achrestos occurs only here in the New Testament.

cites.at: Reformation Study Bible note on Philemon 1:11 (Bible Gateway)

layers.text: Onesimus was a common slave name meaning "useful" or "profitable." Paul plays on it: he was achrestos, "useless," but now he is euchrestos, "useful," to you and to me. Since meeting Christ, he has begun to live up to his name.

layers.evidence: TAGNT: onaimen (G3685), the only New Testament use of oninemi, to benefit, the verb behind onesis, the word Abbott-Smith (in TBESG) derives the name from. Ellicott, Bengel, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Pulpit Commentary hear the name in it; in 1:13 Paul says he would have liked to keep Onesimus with him.
layers.text: Near the end Paul does it again: "let me have some benefit from you in the Lord." Benefit is onaimen, from the verb behind the name Onesimus. Many read it as a gentle hint: the benefit Paul hopes for may be Onesimus himself.

layers.evidence: Christos and chrestos often sounded alike in the everyday Greek of the time, because the vowel eta was coming to be pronounced like iota; the Roman writer Suetonius (Life of Claudius 25) speaks of a Chrestus, often taken to mean Christ. The play is a suggestion some commentators make; Paul does not mention it.
layers.text: Some hear a third play. In the Greek of the day, chrestos, "useful," sounded much like Christos, Christ. Useless, a-chrestos, has become useful, eu-chrestos, through the Christ he met. The letter itself does not point this out.

passages.saying: He learned obedience from what He suffered.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.evidence: Hebrews 4:15 says He was tempted in every way yet without sin. Christians explain how the sinless Son could learn obedience in somewhat different ways; most say He learned it by experience, not by correction.
layers.text: Hebrews says the Son of God did not escape suffering. He prayed "with loud cries and tears," and through what He suffered He learned obedience. This does not mean He had ever disobeyed: the same letter says He "was without sin."

layers.evidence: TAGNT: emathen (G3129) and epathen (G3958). Learning by suffering, pathei mathos, is a famous phrase in the Agamemnon of the Greek playwright Aeschylus, and the pairing became proverbial. Hebrews is written in polished Greek and uses the familiar jingle.
layers.text: The Greek rhymes: emathen, "He learned," and epathen, "He suffered," differ by a single letter. Learning and suffering, mathein and pathein, were a famous pair in Greek wisdom. Hebrews applies the old saying to the Son of God.

layers.evidence: The Pulpit Commentary, Bengel, Poole and Benson take Hebrews 5:7 to refer to Gethsemane (Mark 14:32-42); Barnes says Gethsemane or the cross, and Ellicott and Gill think of the cross.
layers.text: Many hear Gethsemane in the "loud cries and tears" of the verse before. There Jesus prayed, "Take this cup from Me. Yet not what I will, but what You will." On this reading, that is the obedience He learned in suffering.

passages.saying: First, his name means “king of righteousness.” Then also, “king of Salem” means “king of peace.”
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: Hebrews argues that Jesus is a priest of a different and permanent kind, not from Levi's family but "in the order of Melchizedek," who "always lives to intercede."

Genesis gives Melchizedek three verses: king of Salem and "priest of God Most High," he brings out bread and wine, blesses Abram, and receives a tenth from him. The only other Old Testament verse to name him is Psalm 110:4.
Later, in Psalm 110, God swears to David's Lord: "You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek." Hebrews builds its argument on this oath.

layers.evidence: Name meanings from TBESH. The Pulpit Commentary on Genesis 14:18 identifies Salem with Jerusalem. Josephus, Jewish War 6.10.1: the city Melchizedek built, formerly called Salem, was Jerusalem.
layers.text: Hebrews reads the names. Melchizedek joins melek (king) and tsedeq (righteousness), and Salem means peace. The Old Testament names Salem only once more, in Psalm 76:2, in parallel with Zion, so it is usually taken to be Jerusalem.
Jesus Himself raised Psalm 110 in the temple: David calls the Messiah "my Lord." The psalm that seats the Messiah at God's right hand also makes Him a priest forever.
Genesis records no father, mother, birth or death for Melchizedek, and Hebrews makes the silence part of the picture: "like the Son of God, he remains a priest for all time."
Many Christian writers link Melchizedek's bread and wine to the bread and cup of the Last Supper. Hebrews does not mention it.

passages.saying: In the case of a will, it is necessary to establish the death of the one who made it
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAGNT and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the Septuagint, Easton's Bible Dictionary, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Hebrews explains why Christ had to die. He is "the mediator of a new covenant," so that the called may receive "the promised eternal inheritance." And an inheritance comes through a death: "a will does not take effect until the one who made it has died."

layers.evidence: Abbott-Smith (TBESG): diatheke nearly always renders berit in the Septuagint, but in classical Greek means a will. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Gill and Benson read will in 9:16-17 while keeping covenant in view; Ellicott reads covenant throughout.
layers.text: One Greek word, diatheke, is "covenant" in verse 15 and "a will" in verses 16-17. In the Greek Old Testament it nearly always stands for berit, covenant, but in everyday Greek it meant a will. Many hear a play on both senses; some read "covenant" throughout.

layers.evidence: Easton's Bible Dictionary: the Vulgate renders diatheke by testamentum, whence the names Old and New Testament. Barnes: the only place Scripture calls the Jewish books the Old Testament; Gill and the Pulpit Commentary: the books read in the synagogue, Moses being read.
layers.text: This double word named the Bible's two halves. Latin rendered diatheke as testamentum, a will, even where it meant covenant, so the covenants became the Old and New Testaments. Paul once says "the old covenant," for the books of Moses read in the synagogue.

layers.evidence: Bequest: Bengel, who calls it a word fit for one dying and cites Hebrews 9:16. Covenant: Ellicott and Barnes. Abbott-Smith (TBESG) glosses Luke's diatithemi as to assign, and says diatheke is a will in classical Greek but in the Septuagint nearly always stands for berit, covenant.
layers.text: At the Last Supper Jesus says, "This cup is the new covenant in My blood," and "I bestow on you a kingdom." Luke's verb for bestow is kin to diatheke. Some hear Jesus making His will; others hear covenant. The will sense is Greek: Hebrew berit is a covenant.

layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary: the expression comes from Isaiah 63:11, where the Septuagint has ton poimena ton probaton, and the covenant blood from Zechariah 9:11. Also Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Ellicott and MacLaren.
layers.text: Hebrews closes by naming the God who, "through the blood of the eternal covenant," raised "that great Shepherd of the sheep." The Greek of Isaiah 63:11 gives Moses, brought up from the sea, the same title, and Zechariah speaks of "the blood of My covenant."

passages.saying: Jesus Christ, the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, OpenBible.info cross-references, the Septuagint, the NET Bible notes, Easton's Bible Dictionary, Peter Leithart and G. K. Beale, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: John greets the seven churches with grace and peace from God, from the seven Spirits, and from Jesus, named three ways: witness, firstborn, ruler. Then he breaks into praise: "To Him who loves us and has released us from our sins by His blood."

layers.evidence: G. K. Beale, as reported by Peter Leithart (Theopolis Institute, 2011): all three phrases are in Psalm 89:27 and 37. The Septuagint of 89:37 has martys and pistos, witness and faithful; Ellicott also cites the psalm.

cites.at: Peter Leithart, 'Firstborn', Theopolis Institute (2011)

layers.text: All three titles come from Psalm 89, God's oath to David's heir: "I will indeed appoint him as My firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth," and his throne will last like the moon, "a faithful witness in the sky."

layers.evidence: Peter Leithart (Theopolis Institute, 2011): the psalm asks but never answers, and Revelation is about the faithfulness of Israel's God to Israel's King.

cites.at: Peter Leithart, 'Firstborn', Theopolis Institute (2011)

layers.text: Psalm 89 then turns to grief: "You have renounced the covenant with Your servant," and "Where, O Lord, is Your loving devotion of old?" The psalm never answers. Some read Revelation as the answer: David's heir is alive and reigning.

layers.evidence: NET Bible note: the word can mean both witness and martyr. Easton's Bible Dictionary: a martyr bears witness and suffers death for Christ, and the Greek word is elsewhere rendered witness. Abbott-Smith (TBESG): the sense martyr belongs to later Christian writing. The Pulpit Commentary: the same Greek phrase is used of Antipas and of Christ.
layers.text: The Greek for "witness," martys, later came to mean martyr, and gave English that word. Jesus gives His own title to a believer who died for Him: "My faithful witness Antipas was killed among you." Antipas shares his Lord's title, and his Lord's death.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the two oldest manuscripts read freed; the NET Bible note gives it better manuscript support. TAGNT: lousanti in the Textus Receptus and the Byzantine text. MacLaren: washed pictures sin as a stain, loosed as a chain.
layers.text: Copies differ here by one letter. The oldest read lysanti, "released"; others read lousanti, "washed." One pictures sin as a chain, the other as a stain. Revelation knows both: the saints "have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb."

layers.evidence: MacLaren calls Exodus 19:6 the charter of Israel's national life, given right after the exodus. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Barnes and Gill on Revelation 1:6 cite Exodus 19:6, and the Pulpit Commentary notes that Peter's royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9) follows the Septuagint of that verse.
layers.text: The words "a kingdom, priests" come from Sinai, just after the exodus: "you shall be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation." John keeps Israel's order: first freed, then made priests. Heaven sings, "You have made them to be a kingdom and priests."

passages.saying: all its dimensions were equal—12,000 stadia in length and width and height.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the Septuagint, the NET Bible notes, G. K. Beale's work, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: NET Bible note: a stade was about 607 feet (185 m).
layers.text: An angel shows John "the holy city of Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God" and measures it with a golden rod. Its length, width and height are equal, 12,000 stadia each: a cube about 1,400 miles (2,200 km) on a side.

layers.evidence: G. K. Beale (Journal of the Evangelical Theological Society 48, 2005): the city is cubic because only the Holy of Holies was a cube (1 Kings 6:20). The Pulpit Commentary on Revelation 21:16 says the same.

cites.at: G. K. Beale, 'Eden, the Temple, and the Church's Mission in the New Creation', Journal of the Evangelical Theological Society 48/1 (2005)

layers.text: The shape points to one room, the inner sanctuary of Solomon's temple: "twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high," overlaid with pure gold. The city is pure gold too. The holiest room has become the whole city.

layers.evidence: NET Bible note: dwelling place, traditionally tabernacle, literally tent. The Pulpit Commentary, Ellicott and Gill link Ezekiel 37:27 and Leviticus 26:11-12, given on Mount Sinai (Leviticus 26:46).
layers.text: The voice from the throne explains: "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them." The word is skene, a tent or tabernacle. It fulfills God's promise at Sinai, "I will make My dwelling place among you," repeated in Ezekiel.

layers.evidence: Ellicott, Barnes and Benson on Ezekiel 48:35 point ahead to Revelation 21:2-3; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the reality will be best expressed by this descriptive title.
layers.text: Ezekiel's vision of the restored city ends with its name: "from that day on the name of the city will be: THE LORD IS THERE," in Hebrew YHWH shammah. The new Jerusalem is the city whose very name is God's presence.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Ellicott, Barnes, Gill and the Pulpit Commentary compare Ezekiel 48:30-35; the Geneva notes give the gates to the Old Testament and the foundations to the New. Gill on Revelation 21:14 cites Hebrews 11:10.
layers.text: Like Ezekiel's city, its gates bear "the names of the twelve tribes of Israel," and its foundations "the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb": one people of God. It is "the city with foundations" Abraham awaited, "whose architect and builder is God."

layers.evidence: The Septuagint of Exodus 28:17-20 shares eight names with Revelation 21:19-20: jasper, sapphire, emerald, sardius, chrysolite, beryl, topaz, amethyst. Ellicott notes the order differs; Gill and Benson see an allusion. Matthew Henry warns that we are only to take general ideas from the description.
layers.text: The foundations are "adorned with every kind of precious stone," as Isaiah promised. The high priest wore twelve stones for the tribes, and eight of John's twelve are on the Greek Old Testament's list, in another order. Some warn against pressing the details.

layers.evidence: G. K. Beale (Journal of the Evangelical Theological Society 48, 2005): all God's people will have become high priests. MacLaren and Gill also see the high priest's plate here.

cites.at: G. K. Beale, 'Eden, the Temple, and the Church's Mission in the New Creation', Journal of the Evangelical Theological Society 48/1 (2005)

layers.text: Only the high priest wore God's name on his forehead, on a gold plate engraved "HOLY TO THE LORD." In the city every servant of God bears it: "His name will be on their foreheads." What one man wore before the LORD, all His people now wear.

passages.saying: On either side of the river stood a tree of life
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: John's last vision shows a river of life flowing from God's throne through the new Jerusalem, with the tree of life on both banks and its leaves "for the healing of the nations."

The Bible ends where it began. Eden had a river and the tree of life; after the fall the way to that tree was guarded. Now it stands open: "Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life."
The picture also comes from Ezekiel's vision of water flowing from the temple, with fruit trees on both banks that bear every month and leaves for healing.

"No longer will there be any curse" answers the curse on the ground in Genesis 3 and echoes Zechariah's promise that Jerusalem would never again be under the ban (cherem, which BSB renders "utter destruction").

"They will see His face." Adam and Eve hid from God's presence, and Moses was told no one can see God's face and live. Jesus promised that the pure in heart will see God. At the end, what was lost and forbidden is given.
"The Lord God will shine on them" takes up Isaiah's promise: "the LORD will be your everlasting light."
